#7770. Justice Department Announces Results from Operation Not Forgotten 2026

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

The Department of Justice and FBI announced today results of the personnel surge in support of Operation Not Forgotten 2026, which focuses on unresolved cases in Indian country with a priority on cases involving violence against women and children, including those who are missing or murdered.

In its fourth year, Operation Not Forgotten surged personnel and investigative resources across the country from April 1 through September 30, resulting in 118 arrests, 41 individuals charged federally, 25 child victims identified or located, and 72 weapons recovered.  FBI agents conducted 990 interviews and 232 search operations.  Arrests increased by 123% and subjects charged by 52% over 2025.

“The Department of Justice will always work to deliver justice for the victims of violent crime in Indian country,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “Thanks to the hard work of the FBI, our U.S. Attorneys, and other federal and tribal partners, Operation Not Forgotten and Operation Steadfast Promise are helping make communities safer and providing comfort for victims and families.”

“This year’s Operation Not Forgotten continued this FBI’s largest commitment to Indian Country in the history of the Bureau,” said FBI Director Kash Patel. “The results were outstanding – from April 1 through September 30, this FBI worked more than 500 cases, a 59% increase from last year’s operation; 118 arrests, a 123% increase; and 41 subjects charged federally, a 52% increase. This is in addition to 25 child victims identified or located and 72 weapons recovered. These involved life-saving operations, with cases including child sexual abuse, physical assault and abuse, domestic violence, CSAM cases, and more.

“Operation Not Forgotten sends a loud and clear message that our long-forgotten partners in Indian Country are forgotten no more,” said Director Patel. “When I assumed the position of FBI Director a year and a half ago, this FBI promised we would be there for our tribal partners. We have and will continue to be – through our 400 agents dedicated to Indian country, 30 Safe Trails Task Forces, and increased awareness with our Voices Not Forgotten program, where the FBI quadrupled the rewards to at least $25,000 for information associated with homicides, kidnappings and missing persons in Indian country. Thank you to our federal, state, and local partners who continue to work with us to ensure these unsolved crimes and cases receive the surge in resources they deserve.”

“Operation Not Forgotten demonstrates the Trump Administration’s commitment to protecting tribal communities, strengthening public safety, and ensuring that victims and their families have access to justice,” said Billy Kirkland, Assistant Secretary for Indian Affairs, U.S. Department of the Interior. “Through close collaboration across the federal government and in partnership with tribal, state, and local law enforcement, we are bringing additional resources and investigative support to Indian Country to address violent crime, advance unresolved cases, and help families find answers. The Department of the Interior, through the Bureau of Indian Affairs, remains committed to working alongside our partners to deliver meaningful results and build safer communities for generations to come."

Examples of cases charged during this period include:

In the District of Wyoming, the surge resulted in the federal indictment of 18 individuals for an array of violent crimes, and child abuse offenses on the Wind River Indian Reservation, including U.S. v. Jose Benito Ocon: This prosecution arises from an August 2025 incident near Riverton, where the defendant allegedly executed a male passenger with a gunshot to the head inside a moving vehicle before turning the firearm on two female witnesses.  Leveraging the surge’s enhanced investigative assets, a grand jury returned an indictment charging the defendant with five felony counts, including first-degree murder, discharging a firearm during a crime of violence, and two distinct counts of assault with a dangerous weapon. He faces a mandatory sentence of life imprisonment if convicted.  In U.S. v. Darlynn Sheree Seminole, federal prosecutors filed charges following a June 2026 domestic violence intervention by the Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) Wind River Police Department, involving allegations of severe physical trauma inflicted on a 10-year-old.

In the District of Nevada, in July a federal grand jury returned a superseding indictment charging Delshay Astor with the alleged murder of Anna Scott, a member of the Pyramid Lake Paiute Tribe, on the Reno-Sparks Indian Colony in February 2022, and also charged Joel Christy for assisting Astor to avoid apprehension.

In the District of Minnesota, Operation Not Forgotten has resulted in four cases charged during the surge period with violent and sexual offenses in Indian Country, including sexual abuse of minors, domestic assault causing substantial bodily injury, assault by strangulation, and assault with intent to commit kidnapping. One recent case includes U.S. v. Courtney John Barrett Sr. indicted on September 22, 2026, on two counts of sexual abuse of a minor.

In the District of Montana, Michael Plentybuffalo was charged in the death of Shann Nomee, who went missing during an extreme cold snap in January 2024 and whose frozen body was found in a field north of Lodge Grass, Montana after a community led search and a tip to the Bureau of Indian Affairs that pointed to Plentybuffalo.  His case is pending trial.

Also in Montana, Lance Crookedarm was charged with the May 2026 violent assault and non-fatal strangulation of a female victim.

In the District of Arizona, at least four cases were charged including two violent assaults, an arson, and the aggravated sexual abuse of a minor under 12, all of which occurred on the Navajo Nation, as well as an additional assault that was committed on the Fort Apache Indian Reservation.

Operation Steadfast Promise, first announced in 2026, is a continuing comprehensive surge of resources to address a wide range of violent criminal threats impacting Indian country. Operation Steadfast Promise builds on the successes of Operation Not Forgotten with the addition of multiple new initiatives to improve public safety in Tribal communities. The FBI, in coordination with U.S. Attorneys’ Offices, the Bureau of Indian Affairs Missing and Murdered Unit, Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives and Tribal and other federal law enforcement partners, is working across multiple territories to bring investigative aid to cases and resolution for victims and their families. Since Operation Steadfast Promise began in April, the FBI opened over 1,200 new investigations in Indian country, obtained criminal charges on 678 subjects, made over 700 arrests, recovered 2,260 weapons, and made 140 drug seizures.

This year, Operation Not Forgotten continued to address the over 4,000 open investigations in Indian country including death investigations, child abuse cases, domestic violence, and adult sexual abuse investigations, underscoring the persistent and urgent need for sustained resource investment in these communities.

During Operation Not Forgotten, the FBI surged personnel, including investigative, intelligence, and other support personnel, on rotating temporary duty assignments across Indian country in twelve FBI field offices, in Albuquerque, Billings, Detroit, Denver, Jackson, Las Vegas, Minneapolis, Oklahoma City, Omaha, Portland, Phoenix and Salt Lake City. Working in close coordination with Tribal law enforcement agencies, the BIA Missing and Murdered Unit, and U.S. Attorneys' Offices, together law enforcement worked to advance open investigations and pursue accountability for victims and their families.

Additionally, the FBI has brought focus to a new FBI’s Voices Not Forgotten webpage that includes a searchable and interactive map that brings attention to FBI investigations in Indian country where the FBI, in coordination with state, local and Tribal law enforcement are seeking the public’s assistance. In August 2026, the FBI announced the establishment of a new protocol which created a minimum reward of up to $25,000 for all publicly advertised cases involving homicides, kidnappings and missing persons in Indian country where the FBI has assumed jurisdiction.

The FBI remains committed to standing alongside Tribal communities, federal partners, and local law enforcement to address the violent crime threats that continue to impact Indian country. To learn more, visit www.fbi.gov/investigate/violent-crime/indian-country-crime.

The FBI encourages anyone with information related to unresolved violent crimes in Indian country to contact their local FBI field office or submit a tip at https://tips.fbi.gov.

#7768. Yard Eyesores That Ruin Your Curb Appeal

Realtors weigh in on these common yard eyesores that can hurt curb appeal and make a home look less than its best.

What makes a yard an eyesore? It depends on who you ask. Like personal style and hygiene, everyone has different rules when it comes to yard upkeep and design. One person’s cherished garden gnomes might be another’s idea of tacky kitsch. Lawn decor might be a matter of taste, but neglected maintenance like a broken fence or rotting RV in the yard are harder to overlook.

The good news is that nobody has to agree on what makes one yard beautiful and another an eyesore (unless you live in an HOA!), but some yard features are bound to cause a head shake or two from the neighbors. Ahead, find some of the most controversial yard eyesores, with a reminder that curb appeal is always subjective.

Unmowed grass and overgrown weeds make a yard look neglected and can quickly crossover into eyesore territory. But that doesn’t mean everyone’s yard has to look perfectly manicured or exactly the same, either. “A yard that is basic is not a problem as long as it is well kept,” real estate broker Erik Leland says. “You could choose a meadow-style yard or a pollinator garden as long as it is intentional with defined paths and maintained edges.”

Vibrant, healthy trees and shrubs add to a home’s curb appeal, but neglected, overgrown or dead ones can quickly tank it. Even if the rest of the yard is well-maintained, lifeless hedges and trees make it look like an eyesore. “Dead shrubs may appear minor. However, they create a larger perception issue if the property owner is not maintaining something minor, like dead shrubs,” real estate agent Ben Mizes says.

Broken or unused bulky items like patio furniture, piles of lumber, old furniture or broken lawn equipment can quickly pile up in the yard and become an eyesore. Difficult to dispose of, these items can overwhelm homeowners. “When you see clutter and junk in or around a home, it can create stress and uneasiness, even for neighbors,” Realtor Dell Jeanty says. “Keeping the yard organized can make the property and the entire street feel cleaner and more welcoming.”

Fences can add to a home’s curb appeal and value, but a neglected one is just a yard eyesore. Broken, rotting and leaning fences drag down a property’s appeal and give the impression it’s not cared for. However, “a fence does not have to be new to look good,” real estate expert Cameron Walker says. “Old fences can be painted, and neglected and damaged fences can be repaired to make a good first impression.”

Adding statues and garden gnomes to your yard is a personal choice that not everyone will enjoy. What makes you smile may make your neighbor scratch their head. But, even if you are a fan, it is possible to have too much of a good thing. “The right amount of decorations can give personality to a yard and make it inviting, but too many can give a cluttered appearance,” Walker says. “Decorations should be placed to give ample space to display the landscaping.”

While low-maintenance artificial turf is appealing, it can look like an eyesore if not done correctly. Low-quality material and shoddy installation methods result in uneven seams and a cheap aesthetic. “One of the major problems is if it appears as if the grass has been glued to the ground,” Mizes says.  But, even when done right, some people just don’t like the look of fake turf. It comes down to personal preference.

A few carefully placed ornaments can give a yard character, but too many create an eyesore of visual clutter. “A property can lose appeal with an overabundance of various garden ornaments competing for focal points throughout the landscape,” Mizes says. “[But] a collection within a defined area of the landscape can be better appreciated.” Just know that your vision of a beautiful yard might look like a flea market to your neighbor.

“There’s nothing wrong with having garbage and recycling bins in the front yard during pick-up day, but leaving them lined up in front of the house all week doesn’t look great and robs the home of its curb appeal,” Jeanty says. “Tucking them beside the house or behind a small screen keeps the yard looking cleaner.” On the other hand, some folks just don’t see what the big deal is about hiding trash cans and that’s okay, too.

Broken down cars, ATVs or campers strewn in a yard qualify as a yard eyesore in most people’s eyes. Mice settle in, lawn and weeds grow around it and your property can start to resemble a junk yard. It knocks down your curb appeal and impacts your home’s value and your neighbor’s, too. A non-working vehicle doesn’t automatically constitute an eyesore, though, if it’s stored intentionally and preferably out of sight.

While they may spread holiday cheer, not everyone cares for inflatable yard decorations. Where some see whimsy, others see tacky. No matter which side you’re on, most would agree that when deflated during the day, inflatables turn into a yard eyesore. “They just look like piles of plastic in your yard,” Leland says. Additionally, too many inflatables can be fun or make a yard look disorganized and cluttered, depending on your take.

“A derelict shed or rotting play structure is sure to give a bad impression,” Leland says. “If it’s not worth repairing, remove it. An empty space is the better choice.” When I moved into my current home, one of the first things we did was remove a large gazebo that was long past its prime. Our new neighbors all came by and thanked us for removing the neighborhood eyesore.

Kitschy lawn ornaments like plastic flamingos could elicit an eye roll from a neighbor, but perhaps not. “A couple of plastic flamingos can be funny and add personality to a yard, so I wouldn’t automatically call them an eyesore,” Jeanty says. “But when there are twenty of them with mismatched colors competing with signs, flags and other decorations, it becomes a little overwhelming.” Thoughtfully incorporate your outdoor decor into the landscape for a more tasteful display.

#7765. The Best Air Quality Monitors of 2026, Tested and Reviewed

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

By Glenda Taylor, Additional research provided by Tiffany Lewis

Published Nov 15, 2026 9:00 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Indoor air quality monitors can help you breathe easier at home by detecting hazards you can’t see or smell. Gases like radon and carbon monoxide are colorless and odorless but dangerous if inhaled, and these home devices may also identify other pollutants, including volatile organic compounds (VOCs) and airborne particulate matter like dust and pollen. They can serve as a first alert, signaling when to leave an area where the air is unsafe or prompting you to start clearing pollutants and head off health problems. Keep in mind, however, that not all air quality monitors detect all harmful pollutants.

Concerned about the dangers of hidden pollutants lingering in the air of typical homes, we decided to test a number of today’s most popular air quality monitors. We began by extensively researching more than 40 air quality monitors to narrow the field and then selected a range of models to test. (Spoiler: Not all of the air quality monitors we tested earned a spot on this lineup.)

It’s easy to take steps to improve the air quality in your home with an air quality monitor. The best air quality monitor will depend on which pollutants you want to keep track of and whether you prefer a basic or tech-forward model. Our favorite is the Airthings 292 Wave Mini Indoor Air Quality Monitor. It monitors total VOCs (TVOCs), radon, temperature, humidity, mold risk, and outdoor pollen levels. It also comes with smart-home capability and easy-to-use air quality indicators, and it’s suitable for multi-room use.

Ahead, find out what the devices can do and see how the models listed below fared in our hands-on testing to help you choose the best air quality monitor for your home.

Bottom line: Choosing the right air quality monitor depends on specific needs, from detecting VOCs to integrating with smart-home systems.

When it comes to air quality monitors, accuracy is essential. While we didn’t have access to a laboratory for testing, we could offer a measure of control by testing all the monitors under similar situations to see if the readings would correspond when compared to one another. The following monitors all detected the presence of pollutants in our hands-on tests, and we would not hesitate to recommend any of them to help our readers choose a product to detect airborne pollutants in the home.

To measure chemical pollutants in the air without spending a lot, consider the well-priced Wave Mini. The Wave Mini detects TVOCs, humidity, and temperature in the room. After spending a few hours exposed to a dish of oil-based stain in a closed box, the monitor’s TVOC levels spiked. When we compared its temperature and humidity readings to other monitors being tested, the readings were comparable. We believe it accurately portrayed all three readings.

The Wave Mini offers visual indication of air quality in the room, which is accessible when the user waves a hand in front of the monitor. A light flashes green for “healthy,” yellow for “caution,” and red for “poor” air quality.

Users can purchase a hub separately, allowing them to integrate with smart-home products such as Google Assistant and Alexa. The Wave Mini also tracks outdoor pollen levels via the app that syncs with a local weather service. If users don’t have a specific need for monitoring carbon monoxide, radon, or dust, the Wave Mini may be just the right budget-friendly device to keep track of chemical pollutants in the home.

Get the Airthings 292 air quality monitor at Amazon.

Amazon, increasingly offering more of its own brand of products, has entered the air quality monitor field with this device, which measures particulate matter, TVOCs, carbon monoxide, humidity, and temperature. It’s ideal for bedrooms because the small white cube with a little stainless steel vent in front doesn’t have a large display that might keep some folks awake. Instead, a tiny indicator light at the top that shines green, yellow, or red notifies the user of the current air quality. We didn’t find the indicator light to be bright enough to be annoying; it was just bright enough to display the air quality at a glance. However, it only works in a darkened room—it’s not bright enough to see it in sunny daylight.

The Amazon smart air quality monitor syncs with Bluetooth and Wi-Fi, and we found it simple to connect to both. We were unable, however, to connect the monitor to our Echo Show (not included), although it’s advertised as being able to do so. We’re not sure what caused the glitch, since our Echo Show and the monitor individually synced with the Alexa app, but it’s possible it will only connect with newer models of the Echo Show (ours is an older model). Still, the Alexa app on our smartphone provided excellent real-time readings and charts that made it easy to see the air quality.

We tested this monitor in our test box for VOCs and particulate matter. For the first test, we put a dish of oil-based stain in the box, gave it a couple of hours to infiltrate the air, and then checked the app. The VOC reading had spiked. We then opened the box to check the monitor—the indicator light shone red (hazardous air quality). For the second test, we shook the dust mop over the box and monitored the app on our phone. The PM2.5 reading spiked in about 5 minutes and fell 20 minutes later as the dust settled.

To test the CO sensor, we put the monitor in the garage, started the car, and closed the doors. We watched on our smartphone as the CO reading on the app rose. When we opened the garage door, the indicator light was red. We brought the monitor out into the fresh air, and the light turned green in about 10 minutes.

Compared with the other monitors we tested, the Amazon smart air quality monitor’s temperature and humidity readings were right on target. Overall, we liked this little monitor, and we felt it was accurate and discreet enough not to detract from bedroom or nursery decor.

Get the Amazon air quality monitor at Amazon.

This monitor was quite an overachiever in our testing! It connects using Bluetooth technology via the Airthings app and provided detailed reports about our home’s air quality. It will also connect to smart-home devices, such as Alexa, but not via Wi-Fi. Instead, users must download the IFTTT app for their smartphone, which allows a connection between Wave Plus and Alexa.

The first test we performed on the Wave Plus was in a friend’s home where radon was previously detected and is being treated. They have a professional radon detector, so we wanted to see if the Wave Plus would also detect the gas. We positioned it in the basement of the home and left it there for a week.

On our return, we checked the Airthings app and found a radon reading of 3.5pCi/L. This was the exact reading the professional radon detector was showing. When we waved a hand in front of the Wave Plus, it flashed a yellow light that told us the air quality was affected but not hazardous. When we took the Wave Plus outside in the fresh air, the radon level dropped, and the light turned green to indicate healthy air.

We then tested the Wave Plus in our test box where we exposed it for 2 hours to a dish of oil-based stain, a product that contains VOCs. When we checked the monitor, the light was red (indicating hazardous air quality), and on the app we saw that the TVOC reading had spiked. We also compared the monitor’s temperature and humidity readings to those of the other monitors, which were consistent.

We performed one more test—a very unscientific CO2 test. We know that smoke contains CO2, so we took the Wave Plus to the garage and put it on a bench. We used our beehive smoker to blow little puffs of smoke directly on the monitor. The CO2 levels on the app increased slightly, and the indicator light turned yellow. We felt it was detecting some CO2, but we couldn’t tell if it was sensing as much as it should have been. Still, it registered an increase similar to the CO2 detectors on other monitors, so we felt the smoke from the beehive smoker didn’t contain much carbon dioxide.

Get the Airthings 2950 air quality monitor at Amazon or The Home Depot.

The AirVisual Pro air quality monitor by IQAir boasts advanced laser technology, airflow control, and a crafted calibration algorithm to detect precise particulate matter and CO2 data. We felt the most important readings on this monitor for allergy sufferers were the PM1, PM2.5, and PM10 readings. These sensors detect various-size airborne particles, ranging from pollen, which is rather large and can be detected by the PM10 sensor, all the way down to ultrafine dust that can’t be seen but is easily inhaled.

The AirVisual Pro syncs with smart-home systems using either Wi-Fi or IFTTT. We tested both, and both worked well. The best thing about this monitor is its large visual display screen. It’s nice to be able to check the app, but in our opinion, it’s even better to see a visual display at a glance without having to use a smartphone first. Another plus: This monitor gathers outside air quality ratings via local weather reports and displays them prominently.

When we put the AirVisual monitor in our test box and shook a dust mop over it, all three PM sensor readings spiked, which indicated that it was detecting a range of particulate matter sizes. After 30 minutes, the PM10 and PM2.5 readings dropped, as we suspected they would, because the dust had settled. However, the PM1 reading only declined slightly, which we think was due to the extra-tiny particulates that remained airborne longer. The PM1 reading didn’t drop for another hour.

The air quality monitor also detectsCO2 levels, temperature, and humidity. We tested the CO2 sensor by putting the monitor in the garage and blowing puffs of smoke on it from our beehive smoker. The CO2 readings increased slightly, but they didn’t spike. Still, that was consistent with our other monitor tests for CO2.

This specific monitor had some trouble with temperature and humidity, as both readings were off by more than 7 degrees Fahrenheit/points compared to the other monitors. Also, it doesn’t detect VOCs. Overall, this is a handy monitor to detect the presence of primary allergy triggers, such as airborne particulates.

Get the IQAir air quality monitor at Amazon or Walmart.

Those looking for a portable air quality monitor to detect pollen and other airborne particulate matter may find the Temtop P600 air quality monitor to be just the ticket. It uses a Quantum Semiconductor International (QSI) laser diode to detect particulate matter as small as 2.5 microns. A highly sensitive diode also found in professional laboratory equipment, it also detects larger particulates, such as pollen, in the 10-micron range.

The unit has a kickstand that folds out, so users can stand the monitor on a table, nightstand, or even a tent floor when camping out. The first thing we did was charge it fully using the included USB cord, then we started testing.

There wasn’t too much to test on this one, however, since the P600 detects only airborne particulate matter. We put it in our test box and shook a dust mop over it. This monitor doesn’t sync with smart devices, so we couldn’t monitor the readings remotely from a smartphone. Instead, we checked it every few minutes to see if it had changed. The readings predictably spiked after 10 minutes and then gradually dropped (after about 25 minutes) as the dust settled.

One of the upsides to this Temtop model is that it displays air quality over 12 hours on a chart readout. This helped us see air quality changes over the course of a day. Unfortunately, the battery runs down pretty quickly—we had to charge it every morning for a couple of hours in order for it to run the rest of the day. The alternative is to leave it plugged into the USB cord, but the cord plugs into the bottom of the monitor so it won’t sit upright when plugged in. As a solution, we recommend turning the monitor on periodically to check the air quality in a room and then turning it back off to save battery life.

Get the Temtop P600 air quality monitor at Amazon.

Before we chose monitors for hands-on testing, we researched more than 40 models, looking for various sensor types and paying close attention to buyers’ reviews and ratings. We also reached out to an industry expert to get some additional insight. Lisa Townley, the associate director of product management/replacement parts at Carrier, a global provider of HVAC solutions, says, “As people are focused on the health of their indoor environments more than ever before, it’s imperative that they take steps to improve their living and working spaces, including the air they breathe.” She goes on to say that knowing what’s in your air is important because you can “take steps to lower the likelihood of mold … better manage allergens and asthma triggers … and create conditions for improved sleep.” She adds that air monitors with advanced technology to detect finer particles down to 2.5 microns or smaller are particularly useful in the home. We took this expert advice into consideration when choosing which products to test.

For our actual tests—and we must say right off the bat that these were not scientifically controlled trials—we created situations we felt mimicked (or exceeded) real-life air quality problems. To test whether monitors with particulate matter (PM) sensors worked, we put them in a large box and shook a very dirty dust mop over the top. We then monitored the PM readouts on smartphones (or manually) to see when or if they spiked and when they fell (as the dust settled).

We used wood stain, which contains VOCs, including formaldehyde, to test the monitors with VOC sensors. We placed an open dish of oil-based wood stain in the test box and allowed the fumes to infiltrate the box for a couple of hours before checking the readings.

We got a little more creative when testing other sensors! We tested monitors with carbon dioxide (CO2) sensors by blowing puffs of smoke directly on the monitors using our beehive smoker. We tested for carbon monoxide (CO) by putting the monitors with CO detectors in a closed garage with a car running inside. We tested a single monitor to see if it would detect nitrogen dioxide (NO2) by starting a wood fire in the fireplace of our she shed and then closing the flue and monitoring the readout on our smartphone.

To see how well radon sensors worked, we tested them in the basement of a friend’s home, where we already knew radon was an issue.

Temperature and humidity were casually tested by comparing those numbers with other monitors and using the average of the readings (minus the highest and lowest, which we threw out) to determine consistency.

We looked for readout increases and decreases but didn’t compare actual numbers. The detection numbers varied from monitor to monitor from the start, and we felt that one monitor might receive more exposure to a pollutant than another, even though we tried to keep the exposure levels similar. If the readings more than doubled, we deemed it a “spike.”

We also examined and analyzed how easy it was to sync the monitors with Bluetooth; Wi-Fi; or If This, Then That (IFTTT) capability.

To arrive at our awards, we gave models points using a rubric—the better we felt the monitor performed during a test, the more points it received. At the end of testing, we added the points and used them to determine the best category for each monitor.

The monitors we tested ranged from single-pollutant sensors, such as simple radon detectors, to multiple-pollutant detection models that tracked the e humidity levels and several toxic gases. In most cases, a consumer will want a monitor that detects the type of air pollution that puts their home and family at the most significant risk.

For example, consumers who live in a region with known radon problems will want to look for a radon detector or a carbon monoxide detector if they’re concerned about automobile exhaust fumes seeping in from an attached garage. In addition, the following factors are important considerations for consumers shopping for an air quality monitor.

Consumer-quality monitors are not as precise as laboratory detectors, but they’re typically good enough to alert household members that airborne particulates and toxic gases are present.

Monitors that detect dangerous gases, such as VOCs and carbon monoxide, feature electrochemical sensors that react to the presence of gaseous toxins in the air. In some monitors, these sensors must be manually calibrated, but many of the newer models are precalibrated.

Monitors designed to detect dust, allergens, and other airborne particulates do so by estimating the amount of particulate matter that passes in front of a laser. Though valuable, these measurements may not be exact for two main reasons: larger PM might not drift into the laser chamber, and the laser might overlook the tiniest PM.

Home air quality monitors can detect a range of pollutants and will generally detect one or more of the following. Some may detect additional contaminants, but these are the most common.

While some air quality monitors are relatively straightforward, others are pretty high-tech. For example, some models are Wi-Fi capable, and others connect to smartphones and devices via Bluetooth capability or IFTTT technology. Such monitors come with apps that can be downloaded to a smartphone, and then the app walks users through the installation process.

Single-pollutant detectors, such as carbon monoxide detectors, are among the simplest to use because they often just plug into an outlet. If they detect the gas in question, they emit a high-pitched alarm. The best air quality monitor for any individual should be easy to use, depending on the person’s technical skill level. Consumers will want to avoid choosing a complex model with a huge learning curve that requires watching online videos for hours just to figure out how it operates.

Most air quality monitors are relatively small devices, with a sensor unit and a screen that displays how much of the pollutant is currently in the air. Portable units, which fit in a tool belt, purse, or tool bag, are the smallest of all. These are well suited for testing the air on jobsites or in rental homes that don’t have stationary monitors.

Many monitors have the ability to detect numerous problem gases and pollutants and are suitable for multiple spaces. Those who want air quality monitoring to integrate with smart-home technology—so it can display information on a phone or respond to voice commands—will want to look for a smart air quality monitor.

Some people prefer visual alerts rather than numbers or charts that can be challenging to decipher. Today’s monitors often provide color-coded lights that indicate air quality at a glance. Typically, a green light indicates good air quality, a yellow light signifies the air quality is less than optimal but not dangerous, and a red light is a warning that the air quality is poor.

Response time refers to how quickly an air quality monitor will sense the problem and alert the household. Higher-quality devices often have quicker response times because their sensors are more accurate. Response times will also vary depending on which pollutant the monitor is tracking.

For example, some carbon monoxide monitors will sound an alarm after detecting a low level of gas over a few hours; however, if they detect a higher level, the monitor will sound the alarm after just a few minutes. Monitors that measure dust and pollen may not emit a warning at all but simply track and record the varying levels of the pollutants by the hour.

Air quality monitors are either corded (running on electricity from a standard household outlet) or battery-operated (powered by rechargeable batteries). Both are efficient, but for those who need to test air quality in a storage shed or another remote location, a battery-operated model is the handiest.

Very few things are as important as the quality of the air your family is breathing. If you’re new to air quality monitors, you likely have some questions.

According to SmartAir, a developer of air filtration products, the accuracy of air quality readings on monitors falls between 70 percent and 85 percent. While most monitors are as accurate as possible, no single model is 100 percent accurate.

The most common pollutants are airborne particulate matter, such as dust, pet dander, and pollen. However, some other airborne irritants to be aware of are carbon monoxide, lead, radon, and carbon dioxide.

A few simple ideas can improve poor air quality:Clean regularlyKeep your home well ventilatedPurchase an air purifierMaintain your heating and cooling systemsAdd house plantsClean air ductsClean regularlyKeep your home well ventilatedPurchase an air purifierMaintain your heating and cooling systemsAdd house plantsClean air ducts

They sense high or unhealthy levels of particulate matter or toxic gases and alert residents if the levels become dangerous. Many options on the market rely on color-coded air quality indicators to alert users as to the status of the air quality.

Most consumer models can’t detect mold. However, consumers can purchase a home mold test with a petri dish and ingredients that will trigger mold growth if the home has a mold problem. While growing mold may seem counterproductive, it allows consumers to discover whether mold spores are present in the air, so they can take steps to locate the source of the mold and get rid of it.

#7764. Our Amicus Brief in the First Circuit $100,000 H-1B Visa Fee Case

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

It is on behalf of the Cato Institute and myself.

On Thursday, the Cato Institute and I filed an amicus brief in the US Court of Appeals for the First Circuit, in support of California and other states challenging the Trump Administration's imposition of a $100,000 fee on applications for H-1B visas (which are used by tech firms, research institutions, and other organizations to hire immigrant workers and researchers with various specialized skills).

The district court ruling in this case invalidated the $100,000 fee on the grounds that the executive had illegally usurped Congress' power to impose taxes. It relied heavily on the Supreme Court's recent decision in Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, the tariff case I helped litigate. A second federal district court later invalidated the fee on other grounds.

We are very grateful to Deno Hemonas and Philip Wilkinson of Wilson Sonsini Goodrich Rosati, who worked with me on the brief, pro bono. Stanford Law School Prof. and former federal judge Michael McConnell, also worked with us on the brief. He is one of the nation's leading experts on executive power, a prominent conservative originalist constitutional law scholar, and was our lead counsel in the Supreme Court phase of the IEEPA tariff case.

As the Supreme Court emphasized in its recent decisions striking down Donald Trump's Massive IEEPA tariffs, "the Framers gave Congress alone access to the pockets of the people." Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, 607 U.S. 229, 241 (2026)  The tax power was, as Alexander Hamilton explained, "the most important of the authorities proposed to be conferred upon the Union." Just months ago, the Supreme Court in Learning Resources applied those fundamental principles to hold that the President may not use a general grant of authority to "regulate … importation" to impose tariffs, because the power to "regulate" is not the power to tax and Congress did not clearly delegate its taxing power.  This case asks whether the same President—by imposing a tax of his own devising on the entry of noncitizens and calling it a "restriction" on entry—may accomplish by a different label what Learning Resources forbade.

The exaction here is a tax.  Its "defining feature" is that it raises revenue. Learning Resources, 607 U.S. at 241. It is neither a mere fee contributing to the costs of operating the program nor a penalty. The power to "restrict" entry is not the power to "tax" entry.  To limit or qualify entry says nothing about charging for it, and the Government can identify no statute in which the words "restrict" or "restriction" confer tax authority.

The Immigration and Nationality Act  contains express, detailed provisions for fees and payments, setting each amount and specifying how the funds are collected and spent.  This confirms the absence of a generalized, unlimited discretionary presidential taxing power.  Congress does not "hide elephants in mouseholes," and this case involves a very large elephant.  Whitman v. Am. Trucking Ass'ns, 531 U.S. 457, 468 (2001). In more than a century, no President has used Section 212(f) or Section 215(a) of the INA to raise revenue, a point the Government does not dispute.  As the Supreme Court held in Learning Resources, that absence is "strong evidence" the power does not exist.

In addition, the government's interpretation of the relevant statutes violates the major questions doctrine, which requires Congress to speak clearly when delegating power over a major economic or political issue to the executive.  The power to impose unlimited taxes on any visa holders or immigrants entering into the United States is undoubtedly a major one. If, nonetheless, the court concludes that Congress did somehow grant the government the sweeping power it claims, it would violate the constitutional nondelegation doctrine, which constrains delegations of legislative power to the executive.

I have previously criticized the $100,000 H-1B fee on both legal and policy grounds here, here, and here.

NEXT: Today in Supreme Court History: November 14, 1922

Ilya Somin is Visiting Professor of Law at the University of Virginia, Professor of Law at George Mason University, Simon Chair in Constitutional Studies at the Cato Institute, and author of Free to Move: Foot Voting, Migration, and Political Freedom, Democracy and Political Ignorance: Why Smaller Government is Smarter, and The Grasping Hand: Kelo v. City of New London and the Limits of Eminent Domain.

#7763. The Surprising New Guardians Of Liberty And What It Means For The Left

For years, the Left assumed Gen Z would be its most loyal supporters. Young Americans were expected to embrace socialism, distrust our institutions, and see government as the answer to the challenges facing our generation. But that assumption is increasingly being challenged by young people questioning the Left’s worldview and rediscovering the principles that made America exceptional.

The Left’s response has been revealing. Rather than defend its ideas, some of its most prominent voices are threatening the young Americans who dare to oppose them.

Recent remarks by Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-MI) offer a particularly alarming example.

Speaking about holding Trump administration officials accountable, Slotkin described using corruption cases to deter young Americans from joining the administration. She said she wanted prospective employees to worry that serving the Trump administration could mean buying themselves “a ton of problems.” Her stated goal was to discourage young people from getting involved.

Consider what that means for young Americans who want to serve their country by working for an administration, organization, or cause they believe in. The message is that choosing to build a career in the conservative movement could put a target on your back when the opposing side regains power.

>>> Dear Gen Z: Reagan Is Not a Relic

What an abhorrent message. Young Americans should be free to stand up for their convictions and pursue public service without fearing that their political affiliations could make them targets of the Left’s lawfare.

There is a world of difference between prosecuting actual criminal conduct and using the threat of prosecution to discourage participation in the political process. The justice system exists to enforce the law, not to intimidate political opponents or make an example of people whose political affiliations dissent from those in power.

Slotkin may frame her proposal as accountability. But when the stated objective is to deter young Americans from serving their nation, the question is whether the pursuit of justice is being conflated with the pursuit of political power.

Young Americans should find that deeply troubling, regardless of their political affiliation. And for a generation already questioning the Left’s vision for America, these remarks should prompt an even more fundamental question: Why should young people trust a political movement that seems willing to threaten their futures when they reject its ideas?

For years, the Left has presented socialism as a compassionate alternative to America’s founding principles. It promises equality through government control, security through dependence on the state, and progress through the expansion of political power. But beneath those promises lies a fundamental disagreement about human nature, individual liberty, and the proper role of government.

The American experiment rests on a different premise: that our rights come from our Creator, not the government, and that individuals—not political elites—should have the freedom to direct their own lives. Free enterprise, limited government, individual responsibility, and strong families are not outdated obstacles to progress. They are essential to preserving a free and prosperous society.

Socialism asks Americans to place greater trust in government. The American tradition asks government to respect the freedom and dignity of its citizens. One concentrates power in political institutions; the other recognizes that power must be limited to protect individual liberty.

For Gen Z, this is more than an abstract ideological debate. It is a question of what kind of country we want them to inherit—and whether they will be free to shape its future. Will they embrace a system that increasingly looks to government to direct society, or defend a nation built on the belief that individuals should be free to pursue their own aspirations?

The growing willingness of young Americans to challenge the Left’s assumptions should be welcomed as a sign of a healthy republic. No generation is obligated to accept socialism simply because it is presented as compassionate or inevitable. Young Americans have every right to question the Left’s promises, reject its prescriptions, and choose a different path.

>>> The Cost of Growing Up: Why Gen Z Feels Priced Out of the American Dream

At The Heritage Foundation, I see why preparing the next generation to defend America’s founding principles matters. Those principles do not survive on their own. They depend on young Americans who understand what is at stake and are willing to stand up for individual liberty, free enterprise, and limited government—even when doing so puts them at odds with the prevailing political culture.

Conservatives must make that case with conviction. We must demonstrate why the American tradition offers a better vision than the Left’s growing faith in government power. We must also ensure young Americans have the confidence and knowledge to defend that vision on their campuses and in their communities.

But the Left must answer for its own conduct. If its ideas are so compelling, why respond to young Americans who reject them with threats of prosecution? If socialism offers a better future, why should its advocates fear a generation willing to challenge it?

Slotkin’s remarks expose the danger of a political movement that increasingly treats ideological opposition as something to suppress rather than an argument to win. The threat is not simply that young Americans may be discouraged from joining an administration. It is that political participation itself could become a source of fear when the wrong people hold power.

Gen Z does not owe the Left its allegiance, and no political movement has the right to intimidate young Americans into submission.

The future of the American experiment depends on a generation willing to think independently, reject failed ideologies, and defend the freedoms that make this country exceptional. If the Left cannot win that generation through its ideas, it has no business trying to scare it into silence.

#7762. Can You Really Turn Your Riding Lawnmower Into a Snow Plow?

Your riding lawnmower can do double duty this winter by adding a snow plow. Here’s what you need to know before adding a plow to your riding mower.

Snow is considered a “four-letter” word in our home. Living in the northeast, right in the middle of the so called “I-95” corridor, we usually average 20 inches of snow a year. Even with my trusted 26-inch two-stage snow blower and my newest gadget, an 18 volt snow shovel, clearing the driveway and sidewalk can quickly turn into a significant time consuming and dangerous job. If you already own a riding mower (different from a lawn or garden tractor), you may wonder if you can add a snow plow to turn it into a useful piece of year-round equipment.

The short answer is “yes, maybe,” said David Bodzioch, certified Small Engine and Automotive Technology Instructor. Snow (plow) blades are available for certain riding mowers. However, Bodzioch cautioned, “attaching a blade doesn’t necessarily make your mower ready to clean a snow-covered driveway.”

Accessory compatibility, traction, mower size as well as the amount and type of snow you typically need to move will determine if you can, or should, add a plow blade to your riding lawnmower. Before investing in a plow, you need to understand what your mower can realistically handle. As well as determining what accessories you might need. Here’s what our experts have to say about turning a riding mower into a snow plow.

“Yes, many riding lawnmowers can be equipped with a front-mounted snow blade,” said certified Small Engine instructor Jeffrey Cesari. “Even if aftermarket compatible attachments are available, you should use the manufacturer’s approved attachments,” added Cesari. “Adding a plow blade on small tractors requires a set of rear wheel chains and a counterweight for balance,” added Cesari.

For example, John Deere sells a front blade package (as well as snow throwers) designed for specific riding lawnmowers. A John Deer 19 horsepower or better twin-cylinder engine units position the driver closer to the engine for better balance.

What Do You Need to Turn a Riding Lawnmower Into a Snow Plow?

“At minimum, you’ll need a snow blade and direct-fit mounting hardware designed to fit your particular make and model mower,” said Bodzioch. Tire chains and weights should also be considered when operating snow-clearing equipment. According to Troy-Bilt, makers of outdoor power equipment, “Depending on the riding lawnmower mower and snow conditions, the mower will benefit from the added traction that chains and weights provide” when removing snow.

“It depends on whether your mower simply requires a blade, or the added cost of mounting hardware, weights and tire chains,” said Cesari. An add on blade can cost as little as $120 for 22 to 32 inch width universal riding mower plow kit, to over $1400 for a complete John Deere 46 inch front blade snow plow package that includes an adjustable three-position blade height and angle setting you can change from the driver’s seat. Look for heavy-gauge steel blades that are height-adjustable and have the ability to reposition the shave plate for longer life.

The biggest advantage is getting year-round use from expensive equipment you already own. Plus, eliminating the need for another piece of snow-removal equipment that sits unused for nine or ten months out of the year.

“You’ll probably need to buy and install several accessories and that can be expensive,” said Bodzioch. You should also check how difficult it is swapping out the snow blade and grass cutting mower deck. He added that “you also want check if your mower and blade combination are right for your type [concrete, blacktop, etc.] driveway.”

Yes, it can be, and should be, as long as your mower is approved for the attachment, is well-maintained and in good working condition. Following the manufacturer’s operating, maintenance guides and safety instructions is mandatory for safe and efficient operation; the same as when using any other piece of outdoor power equipment.

Bodzioch said, “Proper traction is especially important when driving on ice and snow, or on snow-covered grass or soil.” But Cesari also notes that “you need to be aware of frame structure and that adding a snow plow can cause frame damage, transmission wear and belt fatigue on small home riding mowers.” Cesari said plowing up to five inches should be safe. Always be cautious and use common sense if your mower is struggling while removing any amount of snow.

It depends. It may only make sense if you already own a compatible mower. However, having room and space to safely store the blade should be a real consideration. Cesari added, “Converting your mower to a plow may require buying expensive attachments or accessories. Consider a standalone snow blower or a lawn/garden tractor if it’s difficult swap out the mower deck and plow.” If you regularly deal with challenging snow conditions, a dedicated snow-removal machine may be the better investment.

It depends on how you use the word. While “riding mower” and “lawn tractor” are often interchangeable, there are key differences between the two pieces of equipment. A riding mower typically means any mower you sit on, including a lawn tractor or zero-turn mower. Nevertheless, a lawn/garden tractor will generally be more expensive and have a larger, sturdier frame. Lawn/garden tractors are designed and built to accept manufacturers’ compatible direct-fit attachments and accessories.

Jeffrey Cesari has been teaching Small Engine Technology at Bucks County Technical High School, located in Fairless Hills, PA. for over 30 years. Before teaching, Jeff operated his owned small engine repair shop. Jeff holds a Pennsylvania Department of Education teacher certificate in Small Engine Technology. He also won the prestigious Harbor Freight Tools for Schools Award, obtained a masters equivalence in industrial education. Jef is also a certified PennDoT safety inspector and instructor. Jeff also earned five industry recognized certifications, including 4-cycle and 2-cycle engines, electrical, compact diesel and mechanical systems through the Equipment and Engine Training Council (EETC). (E-mail interview Oct 30, 2026)

David Bodzioch has been an ASE Master Technician for 25 years. Dave is also EETC (Equipment and Engine Training Council) certified and taught Recreational Power Equipment at North Montco Technical Career Center. (Electronic communication Oct 29, 2026)

Also, these heated snowmobile gloves didn’t get wet inside at all after being sprayed with water, and the batteries lasted over 6 hours. We were also able to use our phones while wearing them thanks to their touchscreen-compatible index fingers and thumbs. While the power button is in a different location than many options (the back of the wrist), it was still easy to access and adjust.

Get the Savior rechargeable heated gloves at Amazon, Savior Gloves, or The Warming Store.

Whether you’re inching down bunny slopes or tackling black-diamond runs, these Snow Deer heated ski gloves are designed for serious warmth. Constructed with a water-resistant polyester back and butter-soft leather palm, they feature heating wires that extend across the entire back of the hand to the fingertips. Also, the interior features separate compartments for each finger (essentially a glove inside a mitten), providing a snug, toasty fit.

While the mitten design doesn’t permit much agility, nor does it let you swipe a touchscreen, the supple leather palm proved great for gripping a snow shovel securely. We had precipitation during testing, and our hands stayed warm and dry for the entire 20 minutes we worked outdoors. Even after we came back inside, the batteries continued to output power for another 6 hours.

Get the Snow Deer heated mittens at Amazon or Walmart.

We began by charging the batteries overnight to ensure every pair was ready for a full day of evaluation. We timed how long it took each pair to hit its advertised temperature on both low and high, then tossed them in the freezer for 10 minutes to see if they could actually hold that heat in extreme cold.

To check for water resistance, we sprayed the gloves down, then upped the stakes for waterproofing by putting them in a bowl full of ice for an hour and wearing them outside in the snow. We also wore each pair while shoveling, walking the dog, and using our phones to see how they handled real tasks. Finally, we ran them on low until the batteries died to find the true maximum runtime.

While dependable heat is the primary goal—especially when you’re trying to stay warm without heat—heated gloves must balance insulation with the specific demands of your environment and activities.

Your planned activities will dictate whether you need a heavy-duty glove or a slim liner. For winter sports like skiing or snowmobiling, gloves with a rugged, wind- and waterproof shell will be essential. If you need winter work gloves, a pair with leather palms offers a secure grip. To use your phone or complete detailed tasks, a thin, touchscreen-compatible liner may be the best choice.

Since there’s no universal glove sizing, be sure to measure your hands before buying. When trying the gloves on, your fingers should almost (but not quite) touch the ends, and the wrist cuff should extend far enough to tuck into your jacket sleeves to prevent cold air and moisture from slipping in.

For maximum heat retention and comfort, look for a windproof shell (often made from a polyester blend) combined with a soft interior liner (generally fleece). If you’ll be doing heavy-duty tasks that require a good grip, seek out a pair with durable leather palms and fingertips. Also, be aware that more insulation and padding equal more warmth, but thickness comes at the cost of dexterity.

If your winter activities involve direct contact with snow or ice, waterproofing is essential. Manufacturers typically use synthetic shells made from polyester or nylon to prevent moisture from soaking through. However, complete waterproofing can trap sweat inside, leading to a clammy or uncomfortable feel. To counter this, you may want a pair with a waterproof palm and a ventilated back.

As with heated vests and jackets, most electric heated gloves rely on small rechargeable lithium-ion batteries to provide warmth for anywhere from 2 to 8 hours. If you want heat that lasts through a full day of work or sport, consider buying gloves with removable batteries so you can swap in another set once the first ones become depleted.

While heated gloves have been around for a couple of decades, advancements in battery technology and weather-resistant materials have made them more effective and less bulky. Still, many people have never used heated gloves, so it’s common to have questions. Here are answers to the most frequent inquiries to help you get the most out of these winter workwear essentials.

Yes, heated gloves are worth it if you spend significant time in the cold, have poor circulation, or do outdoor work where maintaining hand dexterity and comfort matters.

Yes, heated gloves are generally safe since they run on low-voltage batteries and include protections like temperature controls and sometimes auto‑shutoff. However, you should stop using them if you feel burning or notice damage to the wiring or battery.

Yes, many heated gloves are machine washable, though you’ll want to check the care tag for specific instructions. Some models require hand-washing, and others can only be wiped down with a damp cloth. Regardless of the method, avoid wringing them out to prevent damage to their internal heating wires.

Many battery-heated gloves can stay warm for up to 8 hours on low before needing a recharge. However, because lithium-ion batteries tend to gradually weaken, you may see battery life decrease as time goes by. Generally speaking, you can charge a typical lithium-ion battery 300 to 500 times before needing to replace it.

Heated gloves should fit snugly but not be restrictive. Your fingers should almost touch the ends, and the wrist cuff should be long enough to tuck into your sleeves. A fit that’s too tight can compress the heating elements and restrict circulation, while a fit that is too loose allows heat to escape.

Most heated gloves warm up within 1 to 5 minutes, depending on the battery voltage and heat setting. Many are designed to get warm quickly on high before being turned down to maintain comfort and preserve battery life.

It depends. Heated gloves are better if you need warmth across your whole hand for extended periods or active use—though they are more expensive. Cheaper disposable or rechargeable hand warmers may be sufficient if all you need is pocket warmth, but they’re really only meant for short outings.

#7760. Religious Liberty, Terrorist Ideology, and the Limits of School Choice

Last year, Texas enacted one of the country's most expansive school-choice policies. The Texas Education Freedom Accounts program now serves more than 100,000 students, enabling families to choose the learning environments that align with their values and best meet their children’s learning needs.

School choice at this scale is worth celebrating. School-choice policies reflect the Constitution’s commitment to religious liberty and America’s longstanding recognition that parents, not the state, are the primary educators of their children.

A century ago, the Supreme Court struck down a Ku Klux Klan-backed Oregon law that would have banned private schooling, ruling in Pierce v. Society of Sisters that “the child is not the mere creature of the state.” Parents, the Court recognized, have the right and primary authority “to direct the upbringing and education” of their children.

Half a century later, in Yoder v. Wisconsin, the Court reaffirmed the “fundamental interest of parents to guide the religious future and education of their children.” The Court declared that only “interests of the highest order” can override these fundamental freedoms.

The Espinoza v. Montana Department of Revenue (2020) and Carson v. Makin (2022) decisions built on that foundation, holding that states cannot exclude otherwise qualified private schools from generally available scholarship programs merely because they are religious. The Court ruled that such discrimination is “odious to the Constitution.”

But Texas policymakers are now facing a question that school-choice advocates cannot avoid: What if parents choose schools funded by foreign adversaries that indoctrinate students to hate people who are not like them, and whose founders and staff have documented ties to terrorist organizations?

>>> School Choice Is About Religious Liberty, Not Just Better Test Scores

What is the limit of school choice?

Earlier this year, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott drew a line when he declared: “There’s no school choice for schools with ties to organizations that have connections to terrorism.” Several months earlier, Abbott had designated the Muslim Brotherhood and the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR) as foreign terrorist organizations. (CAIR is challenging that designation.)

After those designations, acting comptroller Kelly Hancock wrote to Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton asking whether schools with ties to those organizations or the Chinese government could be excluded from the TEFA program. Paxton’s reply was unambiguous: “Let me be crystal clear: Texans’ tax dollars should never fund Islamic terrorists or America’s enemies.” Hancock then announced no schools with such ties would receive Texas tax dollars through TEFA.

That principle—that public funds should not flow to schools with ties to terrorist organizations or hostile foreign powers—is sound. All freedoms have limits. Liberty is not license. A state has a compelling interest in ensuring that taxpayer dollars do not subsidize the indoctrination of children to hate America or to support terrorism.

But even the soundest principle can be implemented in an unsound, or even unconstitutional manner.

In March 2026, Houston-area attorney and father Mehdi Cherkaoui filed a federal lawsuit against Paxton, Hancock, and Texas Education Commissioner Mike Morath, alleging that state officials had “systematically targeted Islamic schools for exclusion based on their religious identity.” His complaint observed that as of early 2026, hundreds of private schools across Texas—including numerous Christian schools—had been approved for TEFA, while not a single accredited Islamic school had been admitted. Cherkaoui sought to use TEFA funds to cover his children’s tuition at the Houston Quran Academy, but the school was not approved under the program. Three Islamic schools and additional parents joined a second suit shortly thereafter.

State officials denied the discrimination charge, explaining to the court that the comptroller’s office “had issues with processing and reviewing schools accredited by the nonprofit Cognia, regardless of whether they have Islamic affiliations.”

U.S. District Judge Alfred H. Bennett was not satisfied with that explanation. On March 17, hours before the original application deadline, he issued a temporary restraining order. At the emergency hearing, Bennett called the complete absence of approved Islamic schools “troubling,” remarking: “If you were to roll dice in a game of chance… you would not come up with those numbers. The appearance of this reeks.” He extended the student application deadline to March 31 and ordered state officials to receive and process applications from Islamic schools through the normal TEFA process. Within days, four Islamic schools were admitted: Brighter Horizons Academy in Garland, Bayaan Academy, Excellence Academy near Plano, and the Houston Quran Academy.

If it is true that the Muslim schools were not approved solely due to their religious affiliation, that would be a clear violation of their First Amendment rights. The Constitution’s guarantee of religious liberty undoubtedly prohibits such blanket discrimination.

However, the story is not so clear-cut. Two of the four schools now receiving TEFA funds—Brighter Horizons and the Houston Quran Academy—are at the center of serious, documented concerns regarding their institutional histories and affiliations.

Brighter Horizons Academy, based in Garland, is a subsidiary of the Islamic Services Foundation. According to a detailed investigation by the Middle East Forum (MEF), the school was established in part by Rasmi Almallah, who served on the board of the Holy Land Foundation—the largest terrorism financing operation in American history—and was named an unindicted co-conspirator in its 2008 federal trial.

ISF’s 2001 tax filings listed Mufid Abdelqader, a convicted HLF official and the brother of senior Hamas leader Khaled Mishal, as vice-president. His niece, Sarah Abdulqader, is currently a teacher at Brighter Horizons, and MEF notes that she “has been a passionate supporter of her convicted Hamas-financing father.” Previous staff reportedly included ISF director Nabil Sadoun, the lead author of ISF textbooks used at Brighter Horizons, a Jordanian Islamist activist whom the Dallas Morning News reported was “deported from the United States in 2010 for concealing Hamas ties on immigration paperwork.”

Some content in those ISF textbooks, used at Brighter Horizons and numerous other Islamic schools, is deeply troubling. According to MEF, one textbook teaches children ages seven and eight that non-Muslims are “the worst of creatures.” Another stresses the importance of jihad [the war against non-believers], stating: “When Muslims gave up jihad, did not abide by God’s will, started fighting among themselves and were submissive in the face of their enemies, God caused them to suffer greatly by allowing them to be dominated by those who do not fear Him or have any mercy for Islam.” The textbooks praise figures listed as unindicted co-conspirators in the Holy Land Foundation terror financing trial, including one who “describes suicide bombers and Hamas terrorists as ‘freedom fighters’ and ‘martyrs.’”

The school’s foreign funding adds another dimension. The Foundation for Defense of Democracies reported that Brighter Horizons received approximately $995,000 from the Islamic Development Bank for construction and expansion. Iran, a U.S.-designated state sponsor of terrorism, holds a significant capital share in the Islamic Development Bank and has representation on its governing board. During the Second Intifada, the bank directly managed funds that were paid to families of Palestinian terrorists who had been killed, injured, or imprisoned.

The Houston Quran Academy is operated by the Muslim American Society’s Katy Center (MAS). Federal prosecutors have described MAS as “the overt arm of the Muslim Brotherhood in the United States.” The academy’s principal, Hamed Ghazali, also chairs MAS’s Council of Islamic Schools. In 1988, Ghazali appeared to solicit funds for organizations later found to have financed Hamas. The next year, he “openly defended calls for the killing of Salman Rushdie.” In 2019, members of Congress called for an investigation into a MAS Philadelphia branch after it hosted an event in which children sang about torturing and beheading Jews.

>>> Stop Writing Blank Checks to Campuses That Protect Hate

These are not isolated cases. Middle East Forum data counts almost 800 Islamic educational initiatives across the United States, of which a clear majority are under Islamist control. Ninety of these institutions are in Texas, and several dozen may benefit from the new school subsidy program. Across those schools, MEF investigators found staff members who have shared Hamas propaganda, praised convicted terrorists, called for the destruction of America, and had children pledge loyalty to the Iranian supreme leader. Much of this infrastructure is tied to foreign money and foreign movements.

These are investigative findings, not criminal convictions against the schools themselves. But they are serious enough that state officials were right to ask questions. The comptroller’s supposed initial approach—a blanket exclusion of all Islamic schools—collides with the Constitution’s guarantee of free exercise of religion. Judge Bennett was right to find that troubling. But a blanket approval driven by litigation is also troubling.

The solution to an overbroad exclusion is not a rubber stamp, but due diligence. States must comply with the Constitution while protecting against terrorism. That requires examining each applicant school on its own record. Some Islamic schools clearly should qualify for the TEFA program. Whether Brighter Horizons and the Houston Quran Academy belong there is a harder question, and one the state should be able to answer through genuine investigation rather than blanket exclusion or court-compelled approval.

States should provide families access to robust school-choice options while protecting religious liberty. State officials should also take their duty seriously to avoid funding schools with genuine ties to terrorism. Those goals are not mutually exclusive. They require only that officials be precise, consistent, and willing to do their homework.

#7759. The Different Police Sirens You Hear Aren’t Totally Random — Here’s What They Mean

Police sirens can sound very different, from a slow wail to a rapid yelp. Here’s why officers switch tones and what drivers should do.

Everyone recognizes an emergency siren. Or do they?

Officers can choose different tones to make their vehicles easier to notice on busy streets or open roads. Some departments also use certain sounds for special warnings. With electronic siren systems offering several options, drivers might hear multiple tones during a single emergency response.

Learn what the common sounds mean, why officers switch between them, whether different tones signal different emergencies, and how drivers should react.

Different police siren sounds serve different purposes, but they don’t necessarily indicate specific emergencies. Officers often switch tones based on traffic conditions or to get drivers’ attention. A faster siren doesn’t always mean a more serious emergency.

The most common police siren sounds include:

Modern police vehicles typically use electronic sirens that allow officers to switch between these sounds. Older mechanical sirens use a spinning mechanism to produce a traditional wail.

Officers also adjust their sirens based on traffic conditions. Faster tones can help get drivers’ attention in heavy traffic, while a slower wail may work on quieter roads. Departments set their own policies for siren use, so there isn’t one standard sound for daytime or nighttime driving.

Regardless of the siren sound, drivers should respond the same way when an emergency vehicle approaches. Drivers should check their mirrors, signal, and safely pull toward the right side of the road to let the police vehicle pass. They should avoid sudden braking or stopping in an intersection.

Anyone already in an intersection should continue through before pulling over. Drivers waiting at a red light shouldn’t enter the intersection unless an officer directs them to do so. After the police vehicle passes, drivers should check for other emergency vehicles before returning to traffic. Specific rules may vary by state.

#7758. Our Amicus Brief in Case Challenging Trump's Section 338 Tariffs Against Canada

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

The Cato Institute and I filed an amicus brief explaining why the tariffs violate statutory requirements, and also run afoul of the major questions and nondelegation doctrines.

Yesterday, the Cato Institute and I filed an amicus brief before the US Court of International Trade, in Gellert Global Corp. v. Trump, the first case challenging Donald Trump's massive 50% Section 338 tariffs against Canadian imports. The plaintiff is represented by the Liberty Justice Center, the public interest law firm I worked with on the case challenging the massive tariffs Trump imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA). That case resulted in the tariffs' invalidation by the Supreme Court earlier this year.

I previously wrote about the Section 338 tariffs and why they are harmful and illegal in an article in The Dispatch, and a paper for the Montreal Economic Institute.

We are grateful to Daniel Cannistra and others at Crowell & Moring for their invaluable pro bono assistance in helping draft and submit the brief on very short notice. Here is a summary of our key arguments, which should soon be posted at the Cato website:

This brief explains why Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 cannot be used to impose the tariffs enacted by Defendants, and why doing so violates the major questions and nondelegation doctrines.

The Court should strike down the Section 338 duties for three reasons. First, Section 338 requires that any tariffs imposed be in response to discriminatory trade restrictions enacted by foreign trading partners, and that those tariffs "offset" the barriers imposed by those countries. The Section 338 tariffs imposed by the Trump administration violate both of these requirements. In addition, Section 338 has been superseded by later statutes and is no longer operative.

Second, the major questions doctrine forecloses interpreting Section 338 to permit the President to impose extraordinary import taxes whenever another country imposes any trade restrictions or declines to purchase American goods. to "speak clearly" when it assigns to the executive "decisions of vast 'economic and political significance.'" The sweeping power claimed by the administration in this case undeniably raises a major question, and it is at the very least unclear that Section 338 actually grants such vast authority.

Third, stripping the statute's qualitative conditions of operative force violates the nondelegation doctrine, which constrains delegation of legislative power to the executive. An extremely high rate ceiling of 50 percent cannot substitute for clear legislative limiting how and when tariffs can be imposed.

Cato and I (together with Prof. Michael McConnell) also recently submitted an amicus brief in litigation challenging Trump's massive Section 301 tariffs.

Ilya Somin is Visiting Professor of Law at the University of Virginia, Professor of Law at George Mason University, Simon Chair in Constitutional Studies at the Cato Institute, and author of Free to Move: Foot Voting, Migration, and Political Freedom, Democracy and Political Ignorance: Why Smaller Government is Smarter, and The Grasping Hand: Kelo v. City of New London and the Limits of Eminent Domain.
