Bottom line: Discover the best snow shovels of 2026, tested for efficiency and ease, with options for every need and expert tips on choosing the right one.

Based on our research and hands-on testing, we’re confident at least one of these shovels will suit your needs. After comparing their features and reviewing what we like (and what we don’t), you’ll be able to find the right tool to make scooping snow easier.

Anyone on the hunt for a solid overall snow shovel will want to give the Shovelution from Snow Joe a look. This combo-style shovel features an 18-inch-wide polypropylene blade with a metal lip and an aluminum handle that snaps together. Its lightweight construction and unique lift-assist handle make scooping and pushing heavy snow across a driveway and lifting snow over a deck railing easy—so much so that even children can help.

Beyond being incredibly lightweight and user-friendly, we also liked that the Shovelution was easy to assemble, especially considering it came in the smallest box. Even though we were pretty uncertain about this shovel before we used it, in the end, our only complaint was that the additional handle was a little awkward when we turned the shovel over for chipping. Even that’s a pretty minor qualm since there’s a convenient strap that holds the handle in place; you just need to take a second to secure it.

What our tester says: “During testing, we didn’t want to like the Snow Joe. The additional lift-assist handle seemed like a gimmick, but it required much less bending over compared to a traditional shovel and plenty of leverage for scooping.”—Zach Lazzari, Product Reviews tester and writer

This reliable and durable shovel from True Temper might be the perfect choice for those with smaller driveways or who live in areas that don’t see a ton of snow. Designed to be a light-duty yet long-lasting shovel, it combines a traditionally shaped 18-inch-wide aluminum blade with a strong steel handle.

During our tests, we found the True Temper aluminum snow shovel to be a great choice for small snowfalls or lightweight snow. It was tough yet light, and we appreciated that we could flip the traditional-style shovel over and chip ice off steps with ease. Also, it doesn’t require assembly, which is a definite benefit if a storm has already dropped a few inches of snow. A few inches is probably all it can handle since the traditional blade shape does make it difficult to carry heavier loads.

Get the True Temper aluminum snow shovel at The Home Depot.

Anyone who’s ever driven over fresh snow and then tried to scoop it afterward knows this can be an impossible task—but the Manplow RevolutionX Snow Pusher is up for the challenge. This two-handled snow shovel features a pusher-style, U-shaped design with a padded grip, a polyethylene blade, and a durable metal handle. This combination allows you to generate some serious force, making it easy to chip up hard-packed ice and snow. Not only that, the design also minimizes bending, which helps prevent both fatigue and back pain.

Though the Manplow has a long list of features and benefits in its pros column, our tests also revealed the shovel’s con. When it came time to scoop and toss the snow we’d unstuck, we found the task nearly impossible. Though there’s a handle attachment to make the job easier, we found it was actually easiest to simply grab another shovel. To be fair, though, that one never could have lifted such packed-down snow.

A heavy-duty snow shovel with a big bucket and metal-edged blade is great, but it won’t be right for every task. When it comes to clearing walkways, this lightweight Emsco Group Bigfoot poly snow shovel is a perfect fit. Simple in form, durable, and easy to grip and lift, it can handle reasonable snowfalls without fuss. During testing, it was our favorite option for clearing our sidewalks and back patio area.

Those who live in condominiums or apartments where small areas need occasional clearing will also appreciate this option. It’s compact, stores easily, and comes in other blade shapes and styles should you need something smaller or larger. Though we found the linked version perfect for clearing light-to-moderate loads without working too hard, a bigger shovel capable of pushing through more volume would be better after big storms.

Get the Emsco Group snow shovel at Walmart.

Though it’s not a replacement for a full snow blower, this surprisingly lightweight and easy-to-handle battery-powered shovel makes short work of clearing walkways, decks, and other tight spaces where shoveling is typically done. During testing, it zipped right through the snow left on our driveway by a big storm, pushing through the accumulated inches with minimal effort. When it came to testing the unit on deeper and heavier snow, we could only remove a few inches at a time. Still, the unit worked down to the ground relatively quickly, and the battery lasted nearly 30 minutes.

When we first held this shovel, we expected more weight. But since its handles are strategically located to balance the head weight, it’s very easy to lift. It’s also easy to use: With the battery charged and installed, you simply push a button to activate the auger.

What our tester says: “Like our pick for Best Overall (also a Snow Joe product), we were initially skeptical about this electric snow shovel. However, just like with that pick, we completely changed our minds after testing.”—Zach Lazzari, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Snow Joe IONMAX snow shovel at Amazon or Target.

We tested the above snow shovels in upstate New York and Montana. Once snow fell in each location, we set to work getting an idea how well these shovels performed.

We used each shovel to clear a sidewalk or other walkway, testing how thoroughly the shovels removed the snow and how easy they were to use. We tested them on a deck to see how well they could toss snow over the railing. We worked each one over a gravel driveway to evaluate whether they could push along an uneven surface.

We also drove over fresh snow before clearing the driveway, packing it down into hard, tire-width trails. We then used all the shovels to push or scoop snow from one side of the driveway to the other, testing how well they could remove packed snow before using the back side of the blade to chip up the icy tire tracks.

Buying the best shovel for snow might seem like a basic task, but as Joe Palumbo, president of Ice Dam Removal Guys LLC, points out, a lot goes into choosing one. “Depending on how much snow you get and what type will determine your best course of action. There are scoops, pushers/plows, ergonomic, and even wheeled ones. One other thing to consider is material. Plastic/poly is my recommendation, and I’d even recommend that you check the lip’s edge and whether it is lined with metal or plastic. Reason being, metal can leave marks on certain pavers, flagstone, natural rock paths, and more.”

The following sections on blade design, materials, handle features, and wheels and maneuverability go into further on what to consider when choosing a snow shovel.

There are three types of shovels intended for snow removal: traditional scoop shovels, pushers, and combination shovels/pushers. The difference mainly comes down to blade design.

Snow shovel blades, which need to be lightweight yet rugged, are routinely made from one of three materials: poly plastic, steel, or aluminum. Each has pros and cons.

A steel or aluminum blade is best for clearing off ice and hard-packed snow because these metals are light yet extremely strong with sharp edges. Metal blades, however, can scratch decking and other wooden or stone surfaces. A plastic blade works well for those spaces and for light to medium snow. Hardy handles typically consist of steel, aluminum, fiberglass, or wood.

Many snow shovels have straight handles, so learning the right grip is important to prevent strain. To shovel safely, place one hand as close to the blade as possible and the other on the handle grip. Some snow shovels boast ergonomic handles, which are curved to lessen the natural tendency to lean over and lift with the back (instead of lifting with the legs).

Another option is an extra “assist” handle closer to the blade, which increases leverage and lifting power. These handles can be a big boost for children (or adults with bad backs), but they’re also all-around helpful for anyone who wants a more ergonomic snow shovel.

Some handles are even cushioned with foam to lessen hand fatigue. Many models feature wide D-grip handles, which, as their name suggests, are shaped like the letter D and provide a firmer and more comfortable grip than a straight handlebar.

If snowfall is particularly heavy where you live, or you have larger areas to plow, a snow removal service might make sense, or you might want to consider a snow pusher or shovel with wheels. Unlike snow blowers, wheeled snow pushers don’t require any gas or engine upkeep, just old-fashioned elbow grease. The wheels make moving and depositing larger quantities of snow a bit easier, while the blade may be made of steel for greater strength, stability, and weight.

In most cases, a plastic shovel for snow will be ideal. They’re generally lightweight, affordable, and durable enough for the heaviest storms—if you purchase a good one.

It depends on the type of snow shovel and application, but the following can serve as a guide:– Traditional shovels should be between 18 and 24 inches wide.– Combo shovels should be around 24 inches wide, though folks with strength concerns will want to go smaller (18 inches).– For push-style shovels, consider the surface. Driveways can benefit from a 36-inch-wide push shovel for snow, while walkways might be easier to clear with a 24-inch-wide snow shovel.

The best time to salt is before the snow falls or after you’ve cleared it away. If you’ve allowed snow to accumulate and become hard-packed or icy, you may need to salt it to melt the ice before you can scoop the slush away, but that’s not ideal. If you don’t have salt on hand but still need help softening snow before shoveling, there are other ways you can melt ice without salt.

Generally speaking, the best time to shovel is after a few inches have fallen. For safety reasons, however, it’s likely best to wait until the morning after the storm to start clearing accumulation.  For more tips, see our guide on how to shovel snow.

Snow shovels are an inexpensive and eco-friendly way to clear away snow before it becomes dangerous ice. According to Joe Palumbo of Minneapolis, Minnesota’s Ice Dam Removal Guys LLC, “It’s always good to have a shovel. Clearing the snow allows any sun exposure to melt and dry the surface, which is much better than having ice there tomorrow.” If you don’t have a shovel but still need to clear away snow, you can try these tricks to remove snow without a shovel.

It depends. A curved or angled snow shovel can reduce the need to bend over and the force required to push snow, which could decrease back strain. Straight shovels are often preferred when lifting or throwing snow, as it’s easier to position your hands on them for optimal power.

#7746. New York’s Property Tax Hike Chases Wealthy Wallets Away

New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani faces an uphill battle balancing the city’s budget while ushering in his very expensive socialist utopia. But rest assured: New public bathrooms and free opera tickets are still coming, and the ultra-wealthy will foot the bill. Or so the plan goes. Predictably, his “tax the rich” mantra is already going beyond New York socialites.

With the pied-à-terre tax implemented in July, property owners and investors who simply maintain a secondary residence in one of the city’s boroughs are subject to a new property tax surcharge. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul proposed it on April 15 to help close the city’s budget gap—the same day Mr. Mamdani posted a video outside Citadel CEO Ken Griffin’s $238 million penthouse, naming him as an example.

The legislature approved the measure on May 27, and it took effect on July 1. It expires June 30, 2031, unless renewed. In the first phase, which runs through mid-2028, condos and co-ops valued at $1 million or more face new, steep tax rates of 4% to 6.5%. For context, New York state’s average effective property tax rate in 2024 was 1.3% and Manhattan’s was 0.71%.

Mr. Mamdani’s “fair share” philosophy includes a quintupling of property taxes on thousands of people. After that initial phase, the surcharge threshold rises to $5 million with lower rates of 0.8% to 1.3% applying to all non-primary residences, exempting housing units under arm’s length leases of at least one year.

>>> No, Mamdani, Socialism Does Not Increase Affordability

Even these lower rates will double people’s property taxes. Furthermore, the lower rates are designed to be offset by new valuation methods being cooked up by the city Department of Finance to increase the assessed value of properties.

The rollout was messy from the start, when the city published a list of 900,000 high-value properties along with many of the owners’ full names. The city appeared to adopt a kind of guilty-until-proven-innocent tax liability, making residents argue they aren’t subject to the pied- à-terre tax. Owners were left with confusion and a loss of privacy.

Since Manhattan has roughly 16,700 condos and co-ops valued above the $1 million threshold, it will be hit hardest by this tax. Secondary residents will owe an average surcharge of $68,559 each year. Brooklyn also shows significant exposure, with the outer boroughs coming in at smaller counts.

New York projects the measure will raise about $500 million in annual revenue. But that assumes the owners stay. Revenue could easily fall by tens of millions of dollars if some owners leave and sell off their secondary residences, which is why wealth taxes elsewhere have repeatedly fallen short of projections. Each property owner who leaves the city shrinks the tax base.

Ultimately, this is a tax on investment in New York real estate with ramifications that will affect even middle-class New Yorkers. Picture a wealthy Californian considering a second residence on the East Coast. At Phase One’s top condo rates, a unit in Manhattan with a $5 million assessed value—the median Manhattan residence is more than $1 million—now has an extra $262,500 tax bill, simply because his primary residence is elsewhere.

>>> Mamdani’s City Grocery Plan Could Leave Taxpayers Paying for Every Banana

Suddenly, Cape Cod and Miami look a lot more attractive, so the wealthy begin taking their spending elsewhere. Local businesses lose sales and need fewer employees. The Real Estate Board of New York argued before the State Legislature that the surcharge would discourage development, reduce construction jobs and drive high-end buyers to other cities.

Supporters argue the tax discourages luxury units from sitting vacant, hence the one-year-lease exemption. But that’s not where New York’s housing crisis is. Very few people can afford $5,000 a month for a one-bedroom apartment downtown. Filling a few luxury units won’t change that.

Legal fights are well underway, and while a Staten Island judge called the rollout “arbitrary and capricious,” the process was ordered to be redone, not canceled entirely. None of the legal challenges has succeeded in striking down the tax itself.

Part-time residents already pay taxes to fund city services, and these surcharges will incentivize those folks to leave, reducing revenue from the surcharge as well as existing taxes. As the more mobile wealthy flee for greener pastures in low-tax states, the burden of funding Mr. Mamdani’s socialist utopia will increasingly have to fall on the less mobile middle class.

#7744. Elissa Slotkin Went to Hungary to Learn How to Jail Her Opponents

Hungary under Prime Minister Péter Magyar has become such a blueprint for leftists’ schemes to persecute and jail opponents the minute they get power that Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin, the leading U.S. proponent of such Gestapo tactics, just got caught on hidden camera admitting she recently came here to take notes.

I came to Budapest for the launch of the book I co-authored with Katharine Gorka, NextGen Marxism. Its fourth translation in Europe, and the stubborn interest in it betrays apprehension about the resurgence of Marxism in the West. While here, I spoke to old friends who expressed consternation about Magyar’s scorched-earth campaign.

To a man, they warned me that what happens here will happen in the United States because the Left here is as blinded with hate about the man Magyar defeated, Viktor Orbán, as U.S. liberals are about President Donald Trump.

“This is the base of Magyar’s party seeking revenge,” writer Gergely Szilvay told me. “They want blood. They want to see as many Fidesz politicians as possible thrown into prison,” he added, referring to Orbán’s party.

News then broke on Townhall late Friday that Slotkin was again caught on hidden cam. Someone secretly filming her asked her on Thursday while she campaigned for an ally in Michigan, “What are we going to do to hold the Trump regime and its collaborators responsible? I’m talking prosecutions.”

“I’m with you,” Slotkin gushed immediately. “So basically, assuming we win both houses, even if we just win one, we’ll come up—we have a list of, like, the ‘signature cases.’”

Slotkin then added enthusiastically here. “I just went to Hungary. I went over to Budapest in Hungary because they just got rid of their authoritarian leader after 16 years. And I’m like, how did you handle 16 years of corruption? We don’t have that much, but we have so much,” she said.

What Magyar did, she said she was told, was “this ‘signature cases’ (strategy).”

One of the first steps Magyar’s party, Tizsa, took was to amend Hungary’s constitution, the Fundamental Law, to ensure that Orbán can never return to office. The amendment limits anyone to two four-year terms as prime minister, retroactive to the return of democracy on May 2, 1990. Tisza could amend the constitution by itself because it won a two-thirds majority in parliament in elections in April.

The law is clearly aimed at one person, Orbán, as it ensures that he can never return as prime minister, an office he has held for 20 years (1998-2002, 2016-2026). In fact, wags here call it “Lex Orbán.”

Magyar then went after the country’s president, Tamás Sulyok, setting aside constitutional niceties to make sure he could bag him. He ousted Sulyok, an Orbán appointee, by again using the two-thirds parliamentary majority to ram through parliament a one-sentence amendment to Hungary’s constitution, the Fundamental Law.

>>> The Surprising New Guardians Of Liberty And What It Means For The Left

The maneuver, unprecedented since Hungary became a democracy after decades of communist tyranny, ended Sulyok’s presidency on flimsy grounds: “serious loss of confidence.” Sulyok had to haplessly sign the amendment or face impeachment, while complaining bitterly about how it violated the rule of law and democratic practices—which it did.

The amendment, said Sulyok, was a “breaking point in Hungarian constitutional democracy.” The “core values of a free society… have been trampled underfoot for the sake of political power,” he added.

But Magyar hasn’t stopped at the prime minister and the president. He is now going after the small fish. My friend Zoltán Koskovics of the Center for Fundamental Rights, which published our book in Hungarian, sent me a long list of Fidesz officials, minor politicians, and businessmen who are now being thrown in prison.

Szilvay wrote in his popular Substack in September that one of the Magyar government’s preferred vehicles for targeting enemies is the newly created National Asset Recovery and Asset Protection Office (NVVH in the Hungarian acronym), whose goal ostensibly is to root out corruption retroactive to 20 years.

This is the usual defense by the practitioners of lawfare here and in the U.S.: We are only going after instances of corruption (or sexual transgressions, or malfeasance in office, or spending state funds on political campaigns, take your pick).

The NVVH, wrote Szilvay, “has the power to launch investigations with unsubstantiated suspicions of the perpetration of a crime. If the NVVH considers that someone has availed themselves of state assets, then a wiretap can be set. It has unrestricted access to tax and business secrets and has been granted the authority to access company premises.”

Government contractors, Szilvay told me, are particularly at risk, no matter how small they are. “Somewhat alarmingly, the NVVH has been given the right to compel anyone to provide information about others—startlingly, this new office has been bestowed with the right to force citizens to inform on others.”

At particular risk are micro enterprises that had government contracts. “A peculiar feature of the traditional Hungarian taxation system led to the expansion of micro enterprises which were easier and cheaper to employ than individuals,” Szilvay writes.

One dimension to all this is that Magyar seems to be acting on orders from the European Union, which is scary considering what Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk did by attacking the Constitutional Court Friday night while the president was overseas.

“Magyar is carrying out orders from Brussels,” Koskovics told me. Szilvay got more specific: “He gets Brussels directives every Friday. That’s why the government announces its agenda on the weekend.”

>>> Viktor Orbán Lost the Election but He Won the Argument

This lawfare, or using the threats of prosecution to go after political opponents, isn’t new. All these things were tried against Donald Trump during his four years in the political wilderness between terms.

In France, Marine Le Pen, the leader of the nationalist-populist Rassemblement National party, may have to wear an ankle monitor while she campaigns for president next year. She is appealing a guilty verdict against her and other RN figures for allegedly diverting European Parliament funds intended for E Parliament RN assistants to the national party.

And in Brazil, Marxist President Inacio Lula da Silva won an election last week that no one expected under very shady circumstances. Seven minutes after the results came in, a pro-Lula Supreme Court Judge, Alexandre de Moraes, issued an order to seize the passport of Lula’s opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro. Bolsonaro was still able to escape, with the help of Argentina and the U.S., using his Italian passport. He is now in the U.S.

The examples around the world are multiplying, as lawfare is now seen as an almost acceptable part of politics, rather than the unseemly retribution and revenge-taking that should be shunned by sophisticated societies.

Slotkin’s scary gaffe while speaking at the University of Chicago in October has been lambasted by Republicans, but she seems to have suffered no setback among her supporters. What’s bizarre is that Slotkin is a former CIA spook, and one thing they are supposed to be good at is keeping secrets. Not Slotkin, apparently.

She’s not alone. Kara Swisher, a podcaster with a large online following on the Left, recently said that the government should go after “Big Balls,” software engineer Edward Coristine, a 20-year-old who briefly worked for Musk’s DOGE.

Magyar’s “signature cases” start with big names, then they’ll be rounding up the 20-year-olds. And Slotkin can’t wait to follow suit here.

#7743. California’s Potential Billionaire Tax Has Already Cost The State

California’s latest proposed tax increase has already led to so much wealth fleeing the state that tax revenue is set to fall, not rise. Golden State politicians announced the upcoming opening day of hunting season on billionaires and are about to find out they can’t fund welfare programs by taxing people who have already left.

At issue is California’s Proposition 40, a one-time 5% tax on billionaires’ net worth, which proponents claim will raise $100 billion for state-funded health care. Unfortunately for them, the wealthy were paying attention. At least seven high-profile billionaires left the state before Jan. 1 of this year, the residency date that determines who owes the tax.

They took with them roughly $539 billion of the state’s $1.9 trillion in billionaire wealth. Google co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin alone shrank the expected haul by $25 billion.

The fact is, $100 billion was never a realistic revenue projection. That estimate ignored losses from departures and legal challenges and both are certain to keep coming. The retroactive residency date alone invites a raft of constitutional challenges.

Supreme Court precedent bars retroactively imposing a “wholly new tax.” Locking people into paying whether they stay or leave, before voters have even approved the tax, burdens the constitutional right to travel. And as the Tax Foundation notes, uncapped penalties on appraisers of hard-to-value assets raise Excessive Fines Clause concerns, since they’re grossly disproportionate to good-faith errors.

>>> California Risks Killing the Golden Goose With Proposition 40

Once departures and litigation are counted, Stanford economists Joshua Rauh and Benjamin Jaros estimate the tax would bring in closer to $30 billion. That’s less than one-third of what was promised, which is bad news for Medi-Cal, the state’s Medicaid program.

But the bigger problem has already arrived. While a wealth tax is collected once, an income tax is collected every year. Rauh and Jaros estimate California’s billionaires pay between $3.3 billion and $5.8 billion in state income tax annually, and every billionaire who relocates takes his share with him permanently.

Weigh that lost income tax revenue against Prop 40’s one-time haul, and the net present value of the tax comes out to negative $38.9 billion.

In other words, the tax is a money-loser for the state. And this estimate isn’t a mere outlier from unlikely assumptions: economists ran 100,000 simulations with different revenue estimates and discount rates, and the state came out behind in 85% of them.

California already depends on a sliver of total earners for most of its tax receipts, with the top 1 percent of earners supplying roughly half of all personal income tax revenue. These are the people creating business, funding startups, and employing thousands of Californians. Losing even a handful of them does real damage to state and family finances alike.

>>> New York’s Property Tax Hike Chases Wealthy Wallets Away

Ironically, the billionaires who flee suffer less than the average Californian. As F. Scott Fitzgerald said, the rich are different from you and me; they can leave for Florida, Tennessee, Texas, or another low-tax state. It’s California’s public services, funded by their income, that will suffer.

Medi-Cal and the other programs counting on this money will still need funding. When $100 billion becomes $30 billion, followed by a permanent reduction to income tax revenue, politicians will clamor for more tax hikes.

But with a shrinking tax base of billionaires, the hikes will inevitably fall on the middle class. A tax sold as making billionaires “pay their fair share” will end up costing the residents not wealthy enough to leave.

Supporters will point to research showing high-earners rarely move because of taxes. But the best-known study examined ordinary income tax rates over many years. A levy on someone’s entire net worth is a different animal and will prompt more people to leave, as seven just did.

Before Californians vote on Prop 40, they should understand how much the tax will realistically raise—and who will get stuck with the actual bill in the long run.

#7741. Overseas Wars Put Affordability on Hold, but That’s Only Temporary

American families aren’t imagining it: we’ve had affordability problems since at least 2022. The situation was improving markedly throughout last year, right up until this February, but overseas conflicts reversed some of that progress. Once the wars with Iran and in Ukraine conclude, affordability will start to improve again.

The cost-of-living crisis started during the Biden administration when prices rose so much faster than earnings that people’s paychecks shrunk in terms of their purchasing power. Although the average American’s weekly paycheck grew roughly 17% during President Joe Biden’s term, it bought about 4% less.

For many families, that meant canceling vacation plans or being unable to buy a newer vehicle. For others, it meant having to put some necessities—like rent, prescriptions and food—on credit cards. Even when inflation came down, families were still facing high costs since inflation is the rate of price increases, not the prices themselves.

To add insult to injury, 40-year-high inflation prompted the fastest rise in interest rates in just as long. Not only did prices rise rapidly, but so did borrowing costs. That was a deadly one-two punch for homeownership affordability as higher home prices and mortgage interest rates combined to double the monthly payment on a median-priced home in just four years.

>>> Today’s Inflation Is Really an Energy Shock

But affordability was improving after January 2025. Real (inflation-adjusted) weekly paychecks rose roughly 2% on average from January 2025 through February of this year. While not a windfall, it was still good progress and reversed half the cumulative losses from the Biden years as income growth outpaced inflation.

Tax and regulatory reform, along with sound energy policy, were spurring economic activity and wage growth while keeping inflation down. Then the Iran war broke out. Global energy markets specifically and supply chains broadly were severely disrupted, causing costs to skyrocket.

Oil prices quickly rose from $60 or $70 per barrel, depending on the market, to $100 or $120. Prices at the pump soon followed, but the energy shock is spilling over to more sectors of the economy with each passing day.

Energy is an input cost in every product and service consumers buy. Food at the grocery store was grown with diesel-powered tractors and fertilizer synthesized from natural gas. It was transported to the store on a truck, and maybe a train too, fueled by diesel. Prices for everything from airfares to plastics to manufactured goods are up because of the energy shock.

The reversal in progress on affordability is evident in housing too. Homeownership affordability hit a three-year high in February and, while still relatively low, marked a significant improvement from the record low in the Biden years. However, it’s fallen each month since then to the lowest level since July 2024 as interest rates ramped up.

Those higher mortgage interest rates are also a result of the current energy shock. When fuel supplies began falling, energy prices rose, and that in turn drove inflation expectations higher. Interest rates followed as lenders demanded a higher return for the anticipated inflation.

And the disruptions are not just from the Middle East, but Eastern Europe too. Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure have exacerbated the shortage of oil and petroleum products, especially diesel. The result was higher prices and lower real earnings.

However, unlike the runaway inflation that peaked in 2022 at an annual rate exceeding 9%, today’s higher prices are not from the government devaluing the currency by spending, borrowing and creating too much money. Rather, this is an energy shock that is causing countless prices to rise.

>>> America Needs Permitting Reform—With No Gimmicks

The difference in causation means there’s a different solution and a better outlook too. The affordability crisis was easing significantly until the energy shocks hit, and those shocks came from overseas. There’s nothing wrong with the domestic fundamentals underpinning the American economy.

Investment is booming. The manufacturing sector is expanding at the fastest pace in at least four years. The private sector is adding jobs. AI is fueling productivity growth and earnings are still growing. Once the conflicts overseas are resolved, energy markets will begin to normalize and costs will start declining. Then the economy will be firing on all cylinders.

Just as higher energy prices are pushing up costs everywhere else, so will lower energy prices put downward pressure on consumer staples everywhere. Likewise, inflation expectations will fall, dragging interest rates back down and improving homeownership affordability. Falling prices and rising earnings mean more breathing room for families.

None of this will happen overnight because supply chains take time to heal, but it’s crystal clear that once peace returns, affordability will follow. All the other pieces of the puzzle are already in place.

#7740. The Mayflower Extract

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Wrapping up the NLC and trying to get home after a groundstop.

The 2026 Federalist Society Convention is a wrap. I have attended every NLC since I was a 1L in 2006 (except for the cancelled COVID year). At each convention, the focus is a bit different but the overall takeaway is similar. There is a healthy a mix of timeless topics and topical topics, with an infusion of the political landscape of the day. It is very hard to capture the essence of a convention by watching some or even all of the panels, as so much business transpires in the hallways and at the bars.

I think much of the press coverage failed in attempt to to consolidate a very broad movement into a few paragraphs. For example, CNN blared "After blue wave, Federalist Society is ready to move on from Trump." Really? Secretary of State Marco Rubio delivered the Olson Lecture, White House Counsel Will Scharf had a fireside chat, White House Advisor May Mailman discussed over-regulation, and Gene Hamilton favored restrictive immigration policy on behalf of America First Legal Foundation. Plus there were other members of the administration from the EPA and OLP.

I think there are a range of opinions about how the conservative legal movement should respond to the current political situation. I don't think anyone actually knows exactly what to do. The midterm election, of course, was the elephant in the room. I offered my take here. A lot can happen over the next two years.

I'm flummoxed by the uproar about the commemorative coins celebrating Calais, Slaughter, and other decision. These were in fact generational wins at the Supreme Court. Justice Scalia established overruling Humphrey's Executor as a founding principle of FedSoc. Since the 1980s, conservatives--including John Roberts--have seen the Voting Rights Act as violating the Constitution. And West Virginia v. B.P.J. was such an obvious outcome--except perhaps at CNN. Plus, this was the swaggiest NLC I've ever been to. There was an entire room to pick up FedSoc swag. The coins were a nice touch.

Perhaps the biggest disruption at the convention was the groundstop. My flight home Saturday evening was cancelled, as were many others. I was able to get a room at the Mayflower for another day. Fortunately, one of the few remaining perks of United status is priority rebooking during "irregular operations." I was originally scheduled to fly home Sunday evening around 7:30 p.m. The United App has a new feature that lets you be on standby for up to three flights at once without losing your confirmed seat. United will send you a text notifying you that a seat opened up on an earlier flight, and you have twenty minutes to accept it. I was able to jump from the 7:30 p.m. flight to the 12:50 p.m. flight. A few hours later, I was given a chance to jump from the 12:50 p.m. flight to the 10:58 a.m. flight. For both of these flights, I was number one on the standby list. Around 5:00 a.m., I was offered the chance to move to the 8:20 a.m. flight, but I was sleeping and missed the window. The system worked very well. And without my status, I doubt I would have been able to get the earlier flight. As things turned out, the 12:50 p.m. flight was cancelled. I will get home today.

NEXT: Today in Supreme Court History: November 15, 1882

Josh Blackman is a constitutional law professor at the South Texas College of Law Houston and the President of the Harlan Institute. Follow him @JoshMBlackman.

#7739. A Midterm Scorecard on the Border and Immigration

Codification of President Donald Trump’s immigration and border policies wasn’t done in two years, with a narrow Republican majority in both houses. After Tuesday, it may be a practical impossibility. But that’s nothing new: The last major immigration reform law passed in 1996.

These days, border and immigration results are driven by the White House, not Congress. So, how do things look today compared with the last midterm elections in 2022?

When it comes to our border, the federal government’s job can be summed up by the Three Ds:

  • Deter inadmissible foreign nationals from entering the United States illegally.
  • Detain them (as the law requires) until their due process is done.
  • Deport them, if the courts so order.

Joe Biden’s administration ditched that in favor of the Three Ps:

  • Process inadmissible aliens and quickly release them into the country.
  • Parole (bypassing visas and other legal means) and induce even more to come.
  • Punt them into the backlogged asylum system, hoping they’ll stay indefinitely.

Trump II jettisoned Biden’s Three Ps and revamped the Three Ds, with quick results.

First, Trump ended the mass parole programs by which Biden brought in almost 3 million aliens and stopped releasing inadmissible aliens arriving illegally at the border. In fiscal 2025, only 691,906 arrived — one-quarter as many as in fiscal 2023. And according to DHS, none were released into the interior. Instead, they were detained and mostly prosecuted for illegal entry.

Second, the Trump administration has increased interior enforcement of immigration law. That means arresting illegal aliens and detaining them during their removal proceedings.

>>> Trump Has Sealed the Border. Now, Democrats Are Hell-Bent on Ending Immigration Enforcement

Essential to keeping this up was a recent ruling by the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals that the government can detain aliens who have not been admitted, even if they’ve been here a while. Three illegal alien plaintiffs, assisted by activist groups, had argued that there is a right to “new process” earned by simply being here long enough. The court ruled that the plaintiff aliens “have received the process due to unadmitted aliens,” and that “procedural due process does not require bond hearings centered on assessing dangerousness and flight risk.”

Simply put, that means the government doesn’t have to go to court every time they detain an alien for removal and explain why. Putting that new burden—which Congress expressly avoided requiring—on the government would massively impede efforts to remove illegal aliens.

A third area of achievement has been ramping up visa vetting and reducing issuance in countries with high fraud rates, weak document integrity, or where nationals often overstay their visas. Coupled with this, the government is finally enforcing the Public Charge rule, designed to prevent indigent aliens from coming here and immediately using taxpayer-funded benefits. Consular officers abroad and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services domestically had long been instructed to minimize such concerns.

Fourth, the Trump administration cracked down on abuse of work visas. Vice President JD Vance called out employers for using H-1B visas to hire cheaper, average-skilled foreign labor while they fire more experienced Americans. Big employers, from high tech to universities, want the cheap labor pipeline kept open, and wages kept lower. But young graduates and skilled American workers don’t want opportunities and jobs taken from them to give to lower-paid noncitizens.

The Department of Justice has investigated companies for discriminating against Americans “by preferring to recruit foreign H-1B visa holders over U.S. workers.” After one effort was shut down by a federal judge, DHS has proposed a $103,265 fee for new H-1B petitions. DHS also wants to charge a $70,000 fee for foreign students to work full-time on their student visas through a controversial program called Optional Practical Training (OPT), with an additional $30,000 for renewals. OPT hires are exempt from certain payroll taxes, allowing employers to save up to 15%. This gives them an incentive not to hire American graduates, even when unemployment among recent graduates exceeds the national average.

The Department of Labor has suspended applications from seven technology companies for abusing the process by which foreign H-1B and other temporary workers become permanent residents, known as PERM. The suspensions included U.S. tech giants and also several Indian outsourcing companies that supply cheaper workers to American companies using visas. Labor also said it was investigating nine U.S. universities for abusing J-1 visas, which are supposedly for exchange programs, to bring in workers.

>>> Combating a Rising Tide of VISA Fraud

While we have seen huge changes in border and interior law enforcement, what hasn’t happened are large worksite raids or enforcement against employers. On this, Trump is being pulled in opposite directions by opposing interests: employers versus American graduates, workers, and his conservative base. At the same time, “sanctuary” policies have made immigration enforcement more expensive, time-consuming, and dangerous, particularly for Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

There are other notable changes since the Biden years. No more planeloads of illegal aliens are being dropped off in U.S. cities in the dead of night by the feds, or busloads sent during the day by border-state governors. State governments aren’t commandeering parks, airports, and even schools to house illegal immigrants. Under Mayor Eric Adams, New York spent billions of tax dollars a year to supply released illegal immigrants with food and other benefits. In 2022, New York’s Roosevelt Hotel was packed with taxpayer-funded illegal aliens. Today, it appears not to be taking any guests at all.

Last but not least, violent crime in America has gone down 25%, according to a Department of Justice survey since last year. One can’t directly attribute that to reduced illegal immigration and the deportation of thousands of repeat-offender illegal aliens, but it’s a fair assumption that removing convicted murderers and thieves leads to less crime.

All in all, Trump has delivered on much of what he promised, though there is more to be done. Meanwhile, the political median among liberals is being pulled even further to the left by the Democratic Socialists of America, towards a policy of zero enforcement. The reduction ad absurdum of this can be found in a recent bill from Rep. Delia Ramirez (D-IL) that would abolish not just ICE but the entire Department of Homeland Security, end all immigration detention, repeal the designation of any terrorist organization, and make deportation almost impossible.

The contrast couldn’t be more stark.

#7737. Americans, Job Market Need Workforce Pell Grants

Millions of everyday Americans are shelling out for unaffordable tuition to get basic workforce credentials. Just look at graduation rates and college debt.

One of the best new solutions is Workforce Pell Grants, which help people get meaningful job credentials—fast.

Workforce Pell Grants are new this academic year. They provide thousands of dollars in funding, depending on the program’s length, to help people earn short-term credentials that directly increase their value in the workforce.

So you can skip the six years of drinking and debt that lead to a dead-end bachelor’s degree in, say, psychology—or no degree at all. Instead, the federal government gives you a monetary incentive to gain useful skills and then get to work.

These education programs are worth it. The ones that get approved must be of high quality. To qualify, they need strong outcomes for completion and employment. This means that no one can set up a fake learning center behind the local laundromat and expect to defraud the government with tuition for a useless credential.

>>> Common-Sense Student Loan Reform Is Finally Coming

States must establish implementation rules and then have programs approved by the federal government. So far, just a few states have gotten programs approved, but we should expect many more. These early days of Workforce Pell Grants offer a terrific opportunity for business partnerships and other innovations.

In Ohio, a bill is moving through the legislature that includes innovative policies to establish qualified education partnerships, or QEPs. Under QEPs, a firm helps a college to design a high-quality degree or certificate program. The college keeps academic control, but the firm can help adapt the content dynamically as workforce needs evolve.

In return, the firm receives a state tax credit equal to 20% of expenses, plus $1,000 for each successful graduate who returns to the industry.

One key is that the graduate can work for a rival firm. The point is to educate the workforce, not to just help one firm.

Because colleges and state systems often lack the resources and industry expertise to stay current, many already work with online program management partners. These are third-party organizations or firms that fill the gap. They move much faster and more efficiently than campus bureaucracies.

QEPs with online offerings and in-person training combine industry wisdom with college structure. Ohio Senate Bill 462 offers a strong policy model that other states should adopt.

Improving the program at the federal level would not be difficult. First, education and workforce agencies should keep feedback lines open. Federal programs are too often one-size-fits-all and hard to adapt to local needs. Let states lead the way, but be open to regulatory and statutory reform as needed.

>>> What the Odd July Jobs Report Means for the Fed

Second, there is a specific way to reduce federal uncertainty over what is allowed. For 15 years, the Department of Education has had a “bundled services” policy that allows firms to group marketing and recruiting services with educational services without violating any rules. Codifying this policy into law would let QEPs thrive without fear of a future anti-business regime.

Third, understanding the effectiveness of Workforce Pell Grants should be a research priority. Are the benefits of the program worth the cost? Should even more resources be moved from four-year college programs into short-term ones?

Finally, members of Congress should resist the effort to “fix” the overall Pell program, both long- and short-term, by simply throwing in more taxpayer dollars to meet the alleged “shortfall” of up to $100 billion over 10 years.

A narrow offset could follow the recent congressional proposal to require students to take at least 30 credit hours per year for maximum Pell eligibility. Or we could end the Public Service Loan Forgiveness program for new borrowers, which could save $30 billion over 10 years.

The United States constantly has millions of unfilled jobs. Ohio has hundreds of thousands. Meanwhile, millions of students are starting college but not finishing it. Workforce Pell Grants are an excellent policy solution that could get even better.

#7735. How "Anti-Zionism" Is Creating Zionists

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

If being Jewish makes one a "Zio," then one must oppose Anti-Zionism if one opposes Anti-Semitism

Joseph Bottum in the Wall Street Journal explains how "Anti-Zionism" turned him into a Zionist.

I am a Zionist because on the ground, activist anti-Zionism is becoming indistinguishable from antisemitism. Whatever linguistic differences exist, whatever distinctions activists say they hold, the metonymy that glides from shouting against Israel to violence against Jews is too easy, too well-greased, for public figures to refuse blame for the rhetoric that allows it. Jews who own restaurants labeled "zio" and "disgusting humans" in Philadelphia, a Jewish center's mural painted over with "Zionism is not welcome" in California, a synagogue's signs defaced with initials for the slogan "All Zionists Are Bastards" in Maryland—the tropes of anti-Zionism slip quickly into the tropes of antisemitism. . . .

I have come to full-blown Zionism—because that is the most coherent way to oppose the activists, left and right, who aim at something profoundly antithetical to the American spirit. "It is now no more that toleration is spoken of, as if it was by the indulgence of one class of people, that another enjoyed the exercise of their inherent natural rights," George Washington wrote in 1790 to a Jewish congregation. "For happily the Government of the United States, which gives to bigotry no sanction, to persecution no assistance requires only that they who live under its protection should demean themselves as good citizens, in giving it on all occasions their effectual support."

This doesn't mean uncritical agreement with everything the government of Israel does. It means that our current forms of activist anti-Zionism would make the U.S. a place wildly different from the one Washington envisioned. . . .

As long as we have a social politics in which antisemitism wears the cloak of anti-Zionism, the duty of Americans is clear: When Jews are targeted as Jews, the solidarity the moment requires from the rest of us is standing up as Zionists.

Jonathan H. Adler (@jadler1969) is the Tazewell Taylor Professor of Law at the William & Mary Law School and a senior fellow at the Property and Environment Research Center.

Artem Stryzhak, 36, a Ukrainian national, was sentenced today to 70 months in prison for conspiracy to commit computer fraud in connection with a series of ransomware attacks that targeted hospitals, government entities, law firms, and other businesses around the world.

“This sentence concludes a years-long, multi-continent investigation into a defendant who participated in cyber-attacks against Americans’ businesses and health care,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “Cybercriminals who terrorize American businesses cannot evade justice by operating from abroad or hiding behind sophisticated technology. Artem Stryzhak’s sentence underscores the Justice Department’s resolve to dismantle ransomware groups, hold them accountable, and protect American businesses and people from cyber extortion.”

“Ransomware attacks like those committed by the defendant wreak enormous havoc — harming victim companies that pay millions in remediation and ransoms, preventing hospitals and other critical facilities from accessing data, and putting sensitive information in the hands of bad actors,” said U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. for the Eastern District of New York. “Today’s sentence reflects that cybercriminals cannot hide from law enforcement and will face significant punishment for their criminal conduct. We remain determined to capture Volodymyr Tymoshchuk, a serial ransomware developer and Stryzhak’s co-conspirator.”

“Disrupting a ransomware group that attacked approximately 1,500 victims worldwide and sentencing a defendant who had targeted healthcare during the COVID-19 pandemic is of significant importance to this office,” said U.S. Attorney Gregory W. Kehoe for the Middle District of Florida. “We are proud of our law enforcement partners for their skilled investigative work in bringing this criminal to justice.”

“Artem Stryzhak is a prolific cybercriminal who worked with multiple ransomware groups to target U.S. businesses and hospitals,” said Operations Director Brett Leatherman of the FBI’s Cyber Branch. “These groups disrupted patient care and caused more than $100 million in losses. Today’s sentence reflects the seriousness of Stryzhak’s crimes and demonstrates the FBI’s global reach and extensive network of international partners. Multiple field offices contributed to this investigation, and our work does not end here. We will continue to leverage every tool at our disposal to track down Stryzhak’s co-conspirators and hold them accountable, including Volodymyr Viktorovych Tymoshchuk.”

According to court documents, Stryzhak, formerly of Barcelona, Spain, conspired with others to perpetrate ransomware attacks on behalf of multiple ransomware groups against victim computer networks in the United States and other countries. The conspiracies caused significant damage to victim computer systems. Beginning in approximately June 2021, Stryzhak joined the ongoing Nefilim conspiracy as a Nefilim ransomware affiliate.  Stryzhak was given access to the Nefilim ransomware and agreed with one of the Nefilim ransomware group administrators, Volodymyr Tymoshchuk, to pay the Nefilim administrators, including Tymoshchuk, 20% of the ransom proceeds extorted from victims in exchange for Stryzhak’s access to the Nefilim ransomware.

The ransomware attacks that Stryzhak conducted with Nefilim ransomware included a June 2021 attack in which Stryzhak stole data from a company in the oil and gas transportation industry. About a week later, Stryzhak created email addresses that were incorporated in a ransom note sent to the victim company. Stryzhak conspired with the Nefilim ransomware actors until at least October 2021. If a victim paid the ransom demand, the perpetrators provided the decryption key, enabling the victim to decrypt files locked by the ransomware.

Also according to court documents, Stryzhak separately joined the Hive ransomware group as one of its earliest affiliates. From June 2021 to January 2023, Hive conspirators attacked approximately 1,500 victims worldwide, including government entities, hospitals, and businesses. Hive ransomware attacks caused major disruptions in victim daily operations around the world and affected responses to the COVID-19 pandemic. In one case, a hospital attacked by the Hive ransomware group had to forgo digital technology to treat existing patients and was unable to accept new patients immediately following the attack.

In his role as a Hive affiliate, Stryzhak and his co-conspirators deployed Hive ransomware against seven victims, including law firms, a dentist office, and a healthcare provider during the COVID-19 pandemic. Victims were unable to access their encrypted data. The FBI, as part of a months-long disruption campaign against the Hive ransomware group, provided a decryption key to one of Stryzhak’s victims, thereby allowing that victim to decrypt its encrypted data without having to pay a ransom.

Stryzhak was arrested in Spain in June 2024 and extradited to the United States in April 2025. Stryzhak pleaded guilty in December 2025 to two counts of conspiracy to commit fraud, extortion, and related activity in connection with computers.

The FBI Springfield Field Office investigated the Nefilim ransomware case and the FBI Tampa Field Office investigated the Hive ransomware case. The Criminal Division’s Office of International Affairs, the FBI’s New York Field Office, and Spanish law enforcement authorities provided substantial assistance locating, arresting, and extraditing Stryzhak.

Acting Assistant Deputy Chief James S. Yoon of the Criminal Division’s Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section (CCIPS), former CCIPS Senior Trial Attorney Brian Z. Mund, and Assistant United States Attorneys Alexander F. Mindlin and Ellen H. Sise of the Eastern District of New York’s National Security and Cybercrime Section prosecuted the Nefilim ransomware case. CCIPS Trial Attorneys Alison M. Zitron and Christen M. Gallagher and Assistant United States Attorney Hannah Watson of the Middle District of Florida prosecuted the Hive ransomware case.

The U.S. Department of State’s Transnational Organized Crime (TOC) Rewards Program has offered a reward of up to $11 million for information leading to the arrest and/or conviction or location of Stryzhak’s charged co-conspirator, Volodymyr Tymoshchuk. #7732. Is Current Second Amendment Jurisprudence Premised Upon a "Misquote"?

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

A New York Times article attempting to discredit Justice Scalia's Heller opinion misfires.

This past week, the New York Times published an article by Mike McIntire and Eli Murray alleging that a "pivotal legal test" for determining whether gun control laws are constitutional is "based on a misquote." Yet it appears it is the NYT's reporters who misfired.

When the Supreme Court begins weighing the constitutionality of assault-weapons bans next month, the justices will be guided by the court's own precedent: a landmark ruling that such restrictions are allowed only if a firearm is both "dangerous and unusual."

For nearly two decades, judges across the country have invoked this language to strike down gun-control laws. It is a pivotal legal test.

Justice Antonin Scalia, writing for the majority in the 2008 case, District of Columbia v. Heller, attributed the "dangerous and unusual" language to Sir William Blackstone, an 18th-century English jurist whose writings became the basis for much of American law.

But in his seminal 1769 treatise, "Commentaries on the Laws of England," Blackstone referred to weapons that were "dangerous or unusual," suggesting that a gun did not need to be both in order to be restricted.

But is there actually an error in the opinion? Here is the paragraph from Heller in which the alleged misquotation occurs, with the allegedly offending sentence underlined:

We also recognize another important limitation on the right to keep and carry arms. Miller said, as we have explained, that the sorts of weapons protected were those "in common use at the time." 307 U. S., at 179. We think that limitation is fairly supported by the historical tradition of prohibiting the carrying of "dangerous and unusual weapons." See 4 Blackstone 148–149 (1769); 3 B. Wilson, Works of the Honourable James Wilson 79 (1804); J. Dunlap, The New-York Justice 8 (1815); C. Humphreys, A Compendium of the Common Law in Force in Kentucky 482 (1822); 1 W. Russell, A Treatise on Crimes and Indictable Misdemeanors 271–272 (1831); H. Stephen, Summary of the Criminal Law 48 (1840); E. Lewis, An Abridgment of the Criminal Law of the United States 64 (1847); F. Wharton, A Treatise on the Criminal Law of the United States 726 (1852). See also State v. Langford, 10 N. C. 381, 383–384 (1824); O'Neill v. State, 16 Ala. 65, 67 (1849); English v. State, 35 Tex. 473, 476 (1871); State v. Lanier, 71 N. C. 288, 289 (1874).

Note that the claim, with the quotation, is followed by a "See" string cite (followed, in turn, by a "See also" string cite of further authorities).  If they were at all familiar with how legal citation works, this should have given the NYT reporters pause. As others have noted, the Supreme Court's style guide indicates that the "see" signal is not used for direct quotations. Rather it indicates that "the cited authority is basic source material supporting, although not stating, the text proposition" (emphasis added). Blackstone is cited first not because it is the dominant source but because the authorities are listed in chronological order.

What makes matters worse is that it appears the authors of the story were informed of all this before the story went to press. One of the story authors contacted John Bash, who clerked for Justice Antonin Scalia the term Heller was decided and worked on the case, and Bash explained all of this to the reporter, as Bash details in this LinkedIn post.  Bash writes:

This is stunning. A recent article in The New York Times claims that District of Columbia v. Heller--the 2008 Supreme Court case holding that the Second Amendment protects an individual right to own a firearm--contains a "misquote" of Blackstone. The supposed misquote is the phrase "dangerous and unusual weapons" in this passage:

We also recognize another important limitation on the right to keep and carry arms. Miller said, as we have explained, that the sorts of weapons protected were those "in common use at the time." 307 U. S., at 179. We think that limitation is fairly supported by the historical tradition of prohibiting the carrying of "dangerous and unusual weapons."

That passage is followed by the signal "See" and numerous citations, the first of which is Blackstone. The Blackstone source says "dangerous or unusual weapons" ("or" instead of "and"), but a number of the sources that follow say "dangerous and unusual weapons," in addition to sources that use the Blackstone disjunctive framing.

Back in October the New York Times reporter reached out to me about this, presumably because I was the law clerk for Justice Scalia on Heller. I immediately wrote back with a full on-the-record explanation of why there was no misquote. Yet the article does not refer to my explanation at all and asserts with no qualification that it was a misquote.

So if anyone is interested, I have posted my email below verbatim. I will also put in the comments my follow-up when the reporter asked me a question.

Here is the e-mail Bash sent to the reporter working on the story:

Hi Mike, thanks for reaching out on this.

Even if I remembered any conversation with Justice Scalia about this particular point (which I don't), it would not be ethical for me to share private conversations I had during my clerkship wth Justice Scalia about the substance of opinions.

But just as an appellate lawyer, I don't see the issue.  If the historical sources are mixed on the conjunctive or disjunctive framing, then it is true that there is an historical tradition of prohibiting weapons that are both dangerous and unusual, the narrower category that is encompassed by either framing.  The fact that Blackstone is the first citation is just because the treatise citations are in chronological order (consistent with making a point about historical tradition), followed by case citations also in chronological order.  The introduction of the treatise list with a "See" signal (rather than no signal) means that the quoted phrase is not necessarily a direct quote from each source (or any source)—as with the "See also" signal for the cases.  And assuming that it's correct that the conjunctive sources all trace back to a single 18th Century treatise, that would not detract from the point that learned commentators had endorsed or applied that test through early American history, which is the point the text is making about historical tradition.

Here is the first follow-up e-mail Bash sent "in response to the reporter asking if he could quote me and whether the opinion purposefully omitted the Hawkins treatise quoted in the conjunctive-framing sources so that Blackstone would be first":

Sure.  Happy to take a look at the quote.

Can't speak to the thinking that went into the opinion, but I really doubt that.  As I mentioned earlier, I don't think the provenance of the limitation is particularly relevant; the point was that commentators had recognized it throughout history.  For example, in a Fourth Amendment case, a court might make the point that the curtilage rule—that the immediate vicinity of the home is considered part of the home—has been recognized through American history, citing late Eighteenth Century and Nineteenth Century treatises and cases.  Even if that rule could be traced back to a single uncited treatise, that's not really the point. It's that courts and commentators endorsed it and so that history and tradition informs the constitutional analysis.

And all that aside, I just think it is implausible that the paragraph would be understood differently if Blackstone had been the second citation rather than the first—especially since Hawkins was himself a very influential legal commentator (if I recall correctly).  I've never heard of a court or litigant attributing weight to the order of sources subject to the same signal (e.g., "See"), which would seem to me especially unwarranted when the sources are presented chronologically (and so there is an obvious explanation for the ordering other than importance).  As I noted before, I think all the sources together make clear a uniform historical tradition of prohibiting dangerous and unusual weapons, the category encompassed by all of their articulations of the rule.

Interestingly enough, the NYT article concludes citing a scholar affirming Bash's contention that, as the relevant passage claims, "there is an historical tradition of prohibiting weapons that are both dangerous and unusual," or as some would put it, those arms that are "unusually dangerous." Insofar as some lower courts have applied a different analysis, it is not clear to me how that is attributable to Scalia's language in Heller, or the contested passage.

The NYT story ends citing a scholar for the proposition that "relying on centuries-old legal precedents requires understanding how earlier generations used language." One might conclude that those writing on the Supreme Court should heed a similar admonition.

#7731. National Security Division Announces First “Near Miss” Non-Prosecution Agreement Under the Department-wide Corporate Enforcement Policy

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

The Department of Justice announced today that it has entered into a non-prosecution agreement with Extreme Networks, Inc.  The company agreed to pay criminal penalties totaling $975,721.84 to resolve the Department’s investigation of sanctions and export control offenses.

The Department reached the agreement under its 2026 Corporate Enforcement and Voluntary Self-Disclosure Policy (“the Policy”), which incentivizes companies to voluntarily disclose discovered misconduct, cooperate with Department investigations, and timely and appropriately remediate the wrongdoing.

This agreement with Extreme Networks marks the Department’s first non-prosecution agreement in a “near-miss” case under the Policy, meaning a case that involved full cooperation and appropriate remediation but did not qualify for a declination of prosecution.  While Extreme Networks’ disclosure to the National Security Division (NSD) was not timely because it occurred under imminent threat of disclosure by a news publication, Extreme Networks nonetheless fully cooperated with the Department’s investigation and timely and appropriately remediated the misconduct. As a result, its disclosure qualified as a “Near Miss” Voluntary Self-Disclosure under the Policy.

“This non-prosecution agreement and million-dollar criminal penalty mark the successful resolution of our investigation into the illegal sale of advanced networking equipment and services to a Russian weapons manufacturer, in clear violation of U.S. sanctions and export controls,” said Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. “The FBI remains dedicated to keeping sensitive technology out of the hands of the Russian military, and we're grateful to Homeland Security Investigations and the Bureau of Industry and Security for their partnership on this case. Let this announcement serve as a clear warning: if you attempt to arm our adversaries by violating U.S. law, justice will find you.”

“HSI remains committed to investigating companies and individuals who evade U.S. export controls and sanctions to provide goods or services to foreign weapons manufacturers,” said Acting Special Agent in Charge Jeremy Pierczynski of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) Detroit. “These laws protect our national security and prevent U.S.-origin products and services from supporting adversaries’ military capabilities. HSI will continue working with our law enforcement and regulatory partners to identify and hold accountable those who undermine these critical safeguards.”

The agreement arose out of an investigation into Extreme Networks’ sales of products and services to Moscow Machinery Building Plant Avangard (MMZA), a Russian weapons manufacturer that was owned by JSC Concern Almaz-Antey (Almaz Antey), which was added to the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List by the Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in July 2014.

Pursuant to the non-prosecution agreement, Extreme Networks will forfeit $487,860.92 in proceeds from the sanctions and export control offenses and pay a criminal fine of $487,860.92, for a total criminal penalty of $975,721.84. Extreme Networks will also resolve a parallel administrative action by OFAC.

Between around March 2018 and March 2022, Extreme Networks, through its then-Russia based subsidiary, Extreme Networks Rus LLC, processed and fulfilled 11 purchase orders for networking equipment and services to MMZA without the required license or authorization from OFAC. MMZA was a primary producer of the S-300 and S-400 anti-aircraft missile systems used by the Russian army. To facilitate these sales, certain Russia-based Extreme Networks employees concealed the identity of MMZA from Extreme Networks’ global trade compliance group, causing Extreme Networks to file false electronic export information via the Automated Export System and smuggle goods from the United States. Through this scheme, Extreme Networks deprived the U.S. government of its ability to carry out its lawful function of enforcing sanctions and export controls designed to protect national security and economic interests. As a result of its unlawful conduct, Extreme Networks earned approximately $487,860.92 in revenue from the sales of goods and services.

Although Extreme Networks’ self-disclosure to NSD was not timely pursuant to the Policy, Extreme Networks nonetheless cooperated with the Department’s investigation by timely providing relevant facts and documents and making employees available for interviews. Extreme Networks also appropriately remediated the misconduct by terminating its contract with the third-party distributor it used to facilitate these sales, improving screening procedures, hiring additional compliance personnel, and implementing diligence procedures in connection with mergers and acquisitions. Given these steps and the lack of aggravating circumstances, the Department agreed to enter into a non-prosecution agreement.

The FBI Charlotte Field Office, the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security, and Homeland Security Investigations investigated the case.

This case was prosecuted by former Trial Attorney Maria Fedor of the National Security Division’s Counterintelligence and Export Control Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Adam Hulbig for the Eastern District of North Carolina.

Election integrity remains essential to ensuring that Americans have confidence in the electoral process. This program will review the 2026 Election Integrity Scorecard, highlighting key results, notable progress, and areas where further work is needed. Experts and state leaders will discuss election reforms, lessons learned across the country, and the challenges and opportunities ahead. The conversation will explore how states can continue strengthening election laws, improving election administration, and promoting transparency and accountability in the democratic process.

RNC, addressing whether documentary proof-of-citizenship requirements are preempted by the National Voter Registration Act and whether noncitizens may be removed from voter rolls during the 90-day quiet period under federal law. Panelists will discuss opportunities for continued reform of citizenship-verification requirements in voter registration and voting.

Join us for a discussion of the current election integrity landscape, the significance of the latest Scorecard results, and how policymakers and election officials can build on recent progress to help ensure elections are secure, fair, and worthy of public confidence.

#7729. The 2026 Russell Kirk Lecture Featuring Dr. Bradley Birzer

From Heraclitus forward, Western civilization has understood the imagination as one of our highest faculties of knowing. We know through our mind (rationality) and through our stomach (passions), but it’s the chest (the heart or the soul) that bridges both. In his lecture, Tolkien, "Lewis, Kirk, Mythos, and Logos," Dr. Bradley Birzer will examine the ways in which imagination has shaped conservatism and tradition, especially through the key figures of Russell Kirk, C.S. Lewis, and J.R.R. Tolkien.

The namesake of the lecture, famed scholar Russell Kirk (1918–1994), established the philosophical foundations of the modern conservative movement with his landmark books, The Conservative Mind (1953) and The Roots of American Order (1974). He was instrumental in the founding of National Review and Modern Age and was a distinguished fellow of The Heritage Foundation.

Kirk’s political philosophy, summarized in his “six cannons of conservatism,” emphasized tradition and convention, transcendence and piety, political prudence, and ordered liberty. His application of those canons to contemporary issues, through essays, lectures, and newspaper columns, was often provocative and controversial, but always noteworthy. Today, his works and legacy are being preserved and advanced by The Russell Kirk Center for Cultural Renewal. The Russell Kirk Lecture Series recognizes eminent thinkers in the tradition of “the father of American conservatism.”
